title: Do not scale Google spend until the offer and page already convert
hypothesis: If we prove the offer and landing page convert before scaling Google, then wasted spend on non-brand campaigns falls because Google captures demand rather than creating it.
does_not_apply_when: store already has a proven offer and a converting page

signal.check: No repeatable conversion rate on the main landing page yet, or no proof the offer sells on any channel.

expected_effect.size: unknown, avoids scaling spend into a funnel that cannot convert

risk.note: Delaying Google spend costs time but avoids burning budget on an unproven page.

prerequisites: a way to test the offer and page on another channel or organically
steps: Check whether the offer and landing page already convert on any channel.
If not proven, pause non-brand Google spend and test the offer elsewhere first.
Keep only tracking, Merchant Center, brand campaigns and one Shopping campaign live while testing.
Move to a full Google build once the page shows a repeatable conversion rate.

test.method: Compare landing page conversion rate before and after the offer test
test.read_point: once the offer test reaches enough sessions to read, or 30 days

title: Build a Google account in this order: offer, page, economics, tracking, structure, bids last
hypothesis: If we fix offer, page and tracking before touching bids and budget, then early wasted spend drops because most owners start in the wrong order.

signal.check: The team's first move on a new or rebuilt account is a bid or budget change, not a check of offer, page or tracking.

risk.note: None; this is a planning order, not a live change.

steps: List the 7 build blocks: offer, landing page, unit economics, goals and KPIs, tracking, structure, targeting, creative, bids and budget.
Confirm each earlier block is solid before opening the next.
Do not set a bid strategy or budget until tracking and structure are checked.

test.method: Track how many blocks were confirmed before any bid or budget change was made

title: Compute break-even ROAS and break-even CPA from contribution margin
hypothesis: If we set break-even ROAS as 1 divided by contribution margin and break-even CPA as AOV times contribution margin, then every bid and budget call reads off real profit instead of a guess.

signal.check: The account has no written break-even ROAS or CPA figure at all.

risk.note: Wrong margin inputs give a wrong target; recheck the inputs, not just the formula.

prerequisites: contribution margin per order after COGS, shipping, payment fees, fulfilment and returns
steps: Pull COGS, shipping cost, payment fees, fulfilment cost and return rate per order.
Compute contribution margin as a percent of AOV.
Break-even ROAS = 1 / contribution margin.
Break-even CPA = AOV x contribution margin.
Write both numbers into the brand record.

test.method: Recompute break-even after each margin input changes and compare against the last figure used
test.read_point: next full margin review, at least quarterly

title: Set every ROAS target from the brand's own margin, never from an industry benchmark
hypothesis: If we set ROAS targets from the brand's own contribution margin instead of an industry benchmark, then the target matches what the brand can actually afford because a 60% margin brand can scale at a lower ROAS than a 25% margin brand.

signal.check: A campaign's ROAS target was copied from an industry average, a competitor or a case study, not from this brand's margin.

expected_effect.size: unknown; higher-margin brands can run profitably at a lower target than lower-margin brands

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: break-even ROAS from contribution margin (GAD-003)
steps: Find every ROAS or CPA target currently set in the account.
Check each one against the brand's own break-even ROAS, not a benchmark.
Replace any target copied from a benchmark or case study.

test.method: Audit every campaign target against the brand's own break-even figure
test.read_point: at the next structure or bidding review

title: Buy new customers at or below first-order break-even only with proven retention data
hypothesis: If we lower the new-customer ROAS floor only when cohort LTV data proves the back end recovers the gap, then acquisition volume rises because the store buys customers it could not otherwise afford.
does_not_apply_when: no measured cohort LTV data
no email or SMS flows in place

signal.check: Measured cohort revenue at 30, 60, 90, 180 or 365 days shows the back end recovers a first-order loss within about 12 months.

expected_effect.size: floor can move to about 0.8x first-order ROAS with strong LTV, or 1.5x to 1.2x if LTV doubles

risk.note: Buying below break-even without real retention data burns cash the back end may not return.

prerequisites: cohort revenue and margin at 30/60/90/180/365 days
email and SMS flows already running
steps: Pull cohort revenue and margin by days since first order.
Confirm the cohort recovers the first-order gap within about 12 months.
Lower the ROAS floor in steps, watching margin on repeat orders, not just revenue.
Stay at or above first-order break-even until this data exists.

test.method: Compare 12-month cohort payback for customers bought under vs at break-even
test.read_point: 12 months after the cohort's first order

title: Raise AOV before cutting costs when AOV is under about $100
hypothesis: If we add bundles, add-ons or a free-shipping spend threshold to raise AOV, then ad profitability improves because a higher order value funds a higher affordable bid.
does_not_apply_when: AOV already over about $100

signal.check: AOV sits under about $100 and margin per order is too thin to fund a profitable bid.

expected_effect.size: a $120 AOV at 10% margin leaves $12 per order, easier to profit from than a lower AOV at the same margin

risk.note: A bad bundle or threshold can hurt conversion rate; test before rolling out.

steps: Build a bundle, buy-one-gift-one, or add-on offer at checkout or the PDP.
Set a spend threshold framed as free shipping, above current AOV.
Test a dollar-off offer only above about $100 AOV.
Measure AOV and units per order before and after.

test.method: A/B or before-after test of the bundle or threshold offer
test.read_point: after enough orders to read a stable AOV change, about 2 to 4 weeks

title: Judge Google by backend revenue and MER, not by in-platform ROAS alone
hypothesis: If we read backend revenue and blended MER alongside in-platform ROAS, then budget stops flowing to a channel that reports high ROAS but does not move total revenue.

signal.check: Google reports rising ROAS while total backend revenue and MER stay flat, or Google is capped as bottom-funnel-only despite real cold search demand.

risk.note: Requires reliable backend revenue and total spend data by week.

prerequisites: total revenue and total marketing spend by week
Google spend vs backend revenue over time
steps: Pull total revenue and total marketing spend by week.
Compute MER (revenue / total spend) alongside Google's in-platform ROAS.
Watch for the overspend pattern: Google ROAS rising, MER flat or falling.
Watch for the underspend pattern: Google capped bottom-funnel-only in a category with real cold search demand.
Decide budget moves from MER and backend revenue, not the platform number alone.

test.method: Weekly comparison of Google in-platform ROAS against blended MER
test.read_point: weekly, over a 90 to 180 day window

title: Fix conversion rate and AOV to win the auction, not just the bid
lever: conversion rate as a bid lever
hypothesis: If we raise page conversion rate or AOV, then the effective bid the store can afford rises because a 2x conversion rate lets it pay 2x per click for the same profit.

signal.check: A competitor consistently outbids the store on Search or Shopping despite similar margins.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a 2x conversion rate supports roughly 2x the affordable CPC

risk.note: None; this reframes where to invest, not a live account change.

steps: Compute the affordable CPC from break-even CPA and current conversion rate.
Compare that affordable CPC against what the auction actually needs to win impression share.
If losing the auction, run a landing page or offer test instead of raising the bid.
Recompute affordable CPC after each page or offer change.

test.method: Landing page or offer test measuring conversion rate change

title: Discount with a margin plan, never a blanket price cut
hypothesis: If we discount only high-margin products or gate discounts behind a spend threshold, then gross profit during the sale holds because the discount does not erase margin on the products it touches.
does_not_apply_when: store already competes purely on lowest price

signal.check: Discounts apply store-wide or on low-margin products without a spend threshold or margin check.

risk.note: A gated or low-margin discount can hurt conversion if buyers expected the old deal.

prerequisites: margin by SKU or collection
steps: List products by margin.
Discount only the high-margin group, or gate the offer behind a minimum spend.
For a premium brand, give a low-cost extra instead of a price cut.
Check gross profit during the sale, not just order volume.

test.method: Compare gross profit per order during the sale against the pre-sale baseline
test.read_point: at the end of the sale period

title: Mine reviews for ad and feed copy angles
hypothesis: If we pull recurring phrases and objections from real reviews into ad and feed copy, then click-through and conversion rate improve because the copy matches how buyers already talk about the product.
does_not_apply_when: store has no reviews and no comparable competitor reviews to read

signal.check: Ad and feed copy is written from the brand's own voice only, with no review language.

risk.note: Only use claims that are true for your own product.

prerequisites: a reviews export, or competitor reviews if the store has none
steps: Export reviews and read for recurring benefits, objections and phrases.
Pull the strongest, most true phrases into headlines and descriptions.
If the brand has no reviews, read competitor reviews for the category and use only claims true for this product.

test.method: A/B test review-sourced copy against existing copy
test.read_point: after enough impressions to compare CTR, about 2 to 4 weeks

title: Keep marketplace revenue separate from Google-driven site revenue
hypothesis: If we tie Shopping bids and brand-defence spend only to the store's own site economics, then Google budget decisions stop being distorted because marketplace price competition never enters the site math.
does_not_apply_when: store sells only on its own site

signal.check: The same SKUs sell on Amazon or Flipkart and the store's own site, and revenue or margin reporting mixes the two.

expected_effect.size: unknown; not measured in this folder

risk.note: No source in this folder covers marketplace-heavy stores; verify against the brand's own data first.

prerequisites: a way to split site revenue from marketplace revenue
steps: Separate site revenue and margin from marketplace revenue and margin in reporting.
Size Shopping bids and brand budget from site economics only.
Do not match marketplace price cuts inside the site's own Shopping feed.

test.method: Compare site-only ROAS before and after separating marketplace revenue from the calculation

title: Add a research stage on YouTube or Demand Gen for a considered, high-AOV purchase
hypothesis: If we add an informational YouTube or Demand Gen stage before Search, then conversion on the eventual Search click improves because a longer research cycle gets a matching funnel step.
does_not_apply_when: low-AOV, impulse purchase category

signal.check: AOV is high and the purchase is low-frequency or considered, but the funnel jumps straight from cold traffic to a Search or Shopping ad.

expected_effect.size: unknown; not measured in this folder

risk.note: No source in this folder covers the funnel build; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: view-through conversion tracking
an informational video or Demand Gen asset
steps: Weight view-through conversions more than click-through in reporting for this category.
Build an informational YouTube or Demand Gen ad ahead of the Search campaign.
Route Search to capture the decision once the informational stage has run.

test.method: Compare Search conversion rate for users exposed to the informational stage vs not
test.read_point: after 4 to 6 weeks of the informational stage running

title: Fix conversion tracking before touching anything else in the account
hypothesis: If we fix conversion tracking first, then every bid, budget and structure decision after it becomes trustworthy because Smart Bidding is no longer flying blind on bad data.

signal.check: No one can state, with confidence, that the primary purchase action is accurate and reconciles with backend orders.

risk.note: None; this is a prerequisite check, not a risky change.

steps: Run the tracking audit checklist (primary action, value passing, enhanced conversions, backend reconciliation).
Fix every failed check before any bidding or budget decision.
Do not run Smart Bidding or PMax until tracking passes.

test.method: Tracking audit checklist pass/fail
test.read_point: before any bid, budget or structure change

title: Set exactly one primary purchase action per account
hypothesis: If we set exactly one purchase action as primary, then reported revenue and ROAS stop doubling because Smart Bidding no longer double-counts a sale.

signal.check: Two or more purchase actions are marked Primary in Goals > Conversions.

expected_effect.size: a second primary purchase action can double reported revenue and ROAS on paper

risk.note: Switching primary actions causes a short relearning period for Smart Bidding.

steps: List every conversion action under the Purchase category.
Set exactly one to Primary; set every other purchase action to Secondary.
Check that ROAS and conversions did not jump after any linking step.

test.method: Check conversions and ROAS before and after the fix for a sudden change
test.read_point: immediately after the fix, then weekly for a month

title: Optimise every ecommerce campaign to purchase, not add to cart or clicks
hypothesis: If we set purchase as the campaign conversion goal instead of add to cart or clicks, then Smart Bidding chases actual revenue because it stops optimizing for a step that does not pay the bills.
does_not_apply_when: a single product at $10,000 to $15,000 with only 8 to 20 conversions a month

signal.check: A campaign's conversion goal is set to add to cart, clicks or another non-purchase action.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: purchase conversion action already set up
steps: Open each campaign's Settings > Conversion goals.
Set Purchase as the only goal.
Remove add to cart, begin checkout, page view, view item and search from account default goals.

test.method: Compare ROAS before and after switching the campaign goal to purchase

title: Never use the GA4 import as the primary purchase action
hypothesis: If we keep the Google Ads tag with enhanced conversions as primary and GA4 as a secondary backup, then reported conversions stop under-counting because GA4 misses about 10% to 20% of Google Ads conversions.

signal.check: The GA4 import is set as the primary purchase action instead of the Google Ads tag.

expected_effect.size: GA4 under-counts Google Ads conversions by about 10% to 20% versus the Ads tag with enhanced conversions

risk.note: None.

steps: Check which purchase action is set to Primary.
If it is the GA4 import, switch the Google Ads tag purchase action to Primary.
Keep GA4 import as Secondary for backup reporting only.

test.method: Compare conversion counts from the GA4 import against the Google Ads tag over the same days
test.read_point: over 7 to 14 days after the switch

title: Turn on enhanced conversions and pass real order value, never a fixed value
hypothesis: If we pass the real order value including discounts and shipping through enhanced conversions, then value-based bidding stops degrading because tROAS is no longer optimizing against a fixed number.

signal.check: Conversion values in recent conversions are identical across orders, or enhanced conversions is off.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a fixed value degrades tROAS accuracy

risk.note: Requires the tag to pass the real order revenue variable; test with a real order first.

prerequisites: a tag or app that can pass per-order revenue
steps: Turn on enhanced conversions with the Google tag method.
Map the value variable to real order revenue, including discounts and shipping.
Map email, phone and address variables for user-provided data.
Place a test order and confirm the value passed matches the order total.
Check the enhanced conversions diagnostics report is clean.

test.method: Compare passed conversion value against actual order revenue for the same orders
test.read_point: after the test order, then weekly for a month

title: Pick the tracking route by spend level: app first, GTM next, server-side above about $50k a month
hypothesis: If we start with the Shopify Google and YouTube app, move to GTM as spend grows, and add server-side tracking above about $50k a month, then tracking accuracy grows with the account instead of over-building too early.
does_not_apply_when: custom_platform without a Shopify-equivalent app

signal.check: The store still relies on a fast app-only setup at a spend level where discrepancies with backend orders are growing.

expected_effect.size: the app gets about 80% to 90% of the way there for a Shopify store

risk.note: Running two purchase actions (app and GTM) at once risks a double primary; keep only one primary at a time.

prerequisites: Shopify admin access
a GTM container for the GTM route
a server container above about $50k a month
steps: Start with the Shopify Google and YouTube app for a new or small account.
Move to GTM plus a Shopify custom pixel when spend or discrepancies grow.
If both the app and GTM purchase actions exist, keep only one as Primary.
Add server-side tracking through Google Cloud or a tag hosting service above about $50k a month.
Reconcile Google purchases against Shopify orders after each route change.

test.method: Reconcile Google-reported purchases against Shopify orders for the same 7 to 14 days after each route change

title: Add the Conversion Linker tag on all pages and turn on auto-tagging
hypothesis: If we add the Conversion Linker tag to every page and turn on auto-tagging, then conversion tracking stops losing clicks to cookie or click-ID gaps because the linker and GCLID handling are both in place.

signal.check: GTM has no Conversion Linker tag firing on all pages, or account-level auto-tagging is off.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: GTM container installed
steps: In GTM, add a Conversion Linker tag triggered on All Pages.
In Google Ads account settings, turn on auto-tagging.
Publish the GTM container and confirm the linker fires with Tag Assistant.

test.method: Check Tag Assistant shows the Conversion Linker firing on every page type

title: Pass product ID, category and value in the dynamic remarketing tag parameters
hypothesis: If we pass product ID, category and value in the tag, then dynamic remarketing and PMax product-level signals work because the parameters they need are actually present.
does_not_apply_when: store does not plan to run remarketing or PMax

signal.check: The tag fires without product ID, category or value parameters, so dynamic remarketing has nothing to show.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: GTM or app-based tracking already installed
steps: Check the tag's data layer for product ID, category and value fields.
Add any missing parameters to the purchase and page view tags.
Confirm dynamic remarketing ads populate with the right products after the fix.

test.method: Check a dynamic remarketing ad preview shows real recently viewed products
test.read_point: within a few days of the fix

title: Set conversion windows to match the purchase cycle, then check them against Shopify
hypothesis: If we set click, engaged-view and view-through windows to match how long buyers actually take to purchase, then reported conversions stop inflating because the windows are not just set to the maximum.

signal.check: Conversion windows are left at the platform default or maximum with no check against actual time from click to purchase.

expected_effect.size: unknown; longer windows raise reported conversions without matching real buying behaviour

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: time from first click to purchase, from backend order data
steps: Pull time from first ad click to purchase from backend or analytics data.
Set click, engaged-view and view-through windows to match that cycle.
Check the resulting conversion count against Shopify orders for the same period.
Adjust the windows if the gap is large.

test.method: Compare Google conversions against Shopify orders before and after adjusting windows
test.read_point: after 2 to 4 weeks on the new windows

title: Track new customers with their own event or a third-party tool, not Google's acquisition setting
hypothesis: If we add a first-order conversion event or read new-customer CPA in a third-party attribution tool, then new-customer growth becomes visible because it is no longer hidden inside a blended purchase number.

signal.check: The account only reports blended purchases, with no way to see new-customer CPA or count by campaign.

risk.note: Leave the customer acquisition setting off; it is not the same as a real first-order signal.

prerequisites: ability to detect a customer's first order in Shopify customer events, or a third-party attribution tool
steps: Add a second purchase event that fires only on a customer's first order.
Option A: make the first-order event primary, keep the all-purchase event secondary.
Option B: keep all-purchase primary and read new-customer CPA in a third-party tool or Google's native new-customer columns.
Leave the customer acquisition campaign setting off.
Check the new-customer count matches Shopify first orders within reason.

test.method: Compare Google's new-customer count against Shopify first orders
test.read_point: monthly, once the event is live

title: Read the last 3 to 7 days on conversion-time columns, not click-date columns
hypothesis: If we add conversion-time columns and read recent days on them, then the store's read of recent performance stops looking artificially weak because Google still credits conversions to the click date by default.

signal.check: Recent-day performance reads are pulled from default click-date columns, and look worse than backend orders for the same days show.

risk.note: None; this is a reporting fix.

steps: Add conversion-time columns for conversions, value and ROAS.
Add a custom ROAS-by-time column (conversion value by conversion time divided by cost).
Read the last 3 to 7 days on these columns instead of the default click-date view.
Never judge the last 1 day on either column set.

test.method: Compare click-date vs conversion-time reads for the same recent days against backend orders

title: Put the ad account, Merchant Center and analytics under one master login
hypothesis: If we consolidate Google Ads, Merchant Center and analytics under one master account, then feed, ratings and purchase data reconcile correctly because they all sit under the same owner.
does_not_apply_when: account already consolidated under one master login

signal.check: Google Ads, Merchant Center and analytics are owned or accessed by different logins or agencies.

risk.note: Changing account ownership can briefly disrupt links; do it during a low-traffic window.

steps: Identify who currently owns Google Ads, Merchant Center and the analytics property.
Consolidate ownership or admin access under one master Google account.
Re-link Merchant Center, GA4 and Google Ads under that master account.

test.method: Confirm all three products show the same owner and links resolve without error

title: Reconcile Google-reported purchases with backend orders after setup and monthly
hypothesis: If we reconcile Google purchases with Shopify orders monthly, then a silent tracking break gets caught early because the two numbers are checked against each other on a schedule.

signal.check: No standing monthly check compares Google-reported purchases with backend orders for the same days.

expected_effect.size: no numeric match threshold is given; track the gap over time instead

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: backend orders and revenue by day
steps: Pull Google purchases (conversion time) and Shopify orders for the same 7 to 14 days.
Compare counts and revenue.
Investigate any large or growing gap (windows, tag, consent, duplicates).
Repeat monthly.

test.method: Track the reconciliation gap month over month

title: Track subscription first-order value and subscription LTV as separate signals
hypothesis: If we track first-order value and subscription LTV as two separate conversion signals, then tCPA or Maximize Conversion Value stops chasing the wrong number because it is not blending a one-time sale with recurring value.
does_not_apply_when: one_off

signal.check: A subscription or repeat-box brand reports one blended purchase value with no separate first-order or subscription LTV signal.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives the tracking build

risk.note: No library source gives the tracking build; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: subscription platform data on renewal value
steps: Add a first-order value conversion signal separate from renewal value.
Add a subscription LTV signal fed from the subscription platform.
Point tCPA or Maximize Conversion Value at the signal that matches the campaign's real goal.

test.method: Compare bidding behaviour before and after separating the two signals
test.read_point: after one full bidding cycle, about 30 days

title: Set up Merchant Center for every store with real policies and a real brand experience
hypothesis: If we set up Merchant Center properly, then Shopping, PMax with products, and Demand Gen with feed all become possible because they require a Merchant Center link to run.
does_not_apply_when: a gray-hat, non-compliant or heavy dropshipping store that would get banned

signal.check: No Merchant Center account exists, or Shopping and PMax with products cannot run.

risk.note: None; setup is reversible by fixing issues in place.

prerequisites: business info, shipping and returns policy, product catalog
steps: Create or claim the Merchant Center account.
Complete business information, website verification, shipping and returns, tax.
Add the product feed and confirm products import.

test.method: Confirm products show Approved status and Shopping campaigns become available
test.read_point: 1 to 2 weeks after setup, allowing for approval time

title: Match Merchant Center business info exactly to the live site
hypothesis: If we keep shipping, returns and contact details identical between Merchant Center and the site, then suspension risk drops because mismatches are the top suspension trigger.

signal.check: Merchant Center shipping speed, cost, courier names or returns window differ from what the site actually shows.

expected_effect.size: a client who changed courier without updating Merchant Center was suspended for about a week

risk.note: A missed update after a courier or policy change is the most common trigger.

steps: Compare Merchant Center shipping and returns settings against the live site line by line.
Name couriers explicitly and link directly to the returns policy page.
Set the Shopify shipping sync to manual so site changes do not silently create a mismatch.
Update Merchant Center the same day a courier or shipping cost changes.

test.method: Run the site-vs-Merchant-Center match check monthly

title: Enroll the 4 Merchant Center add-ons: remarketing, reviews, ratings, promotions
hypothesis: If we enroll dynamic remarketing, Google customer reviews, product ratings and promotions, then listings show more trust signals because the add-ons are active, not just available.
does_not_apply_when: store has under 50 total reviews and cannot reach 3 per product yet, for the ratings add-on only

signal.check: Settings > Add-ons shows one or more of the 4 add-ons as available but not active.

expected_effect.size: unknown; product ratings need 2 to 4 weeks to show once eligible

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: at least 50 total reviews and 3 per product for ratings to show
steps: Open Settings > Add-ons > Discover.
Enroll dynamic remarketing, Google customer reviews, product ratings and promotions.
Connect a reviews source: Google Customer Reviews, an official aggregator like Trustpilot or Stamped, or Judge.me through Shopify.
Check each add-on is Active, not only Available.

test.method: Check add-on status and whether ratings display on listings

title: Never edit price, availability or product ID in Merchant Center directly
lever: single source of truth for price
hypothesis: If we always change price, availability and stock in Shopify and let the feed sync, then price mismatches disappear because Merchant Center never holds an out-of-sync manual edit.

signal.check: Someone edits price, availability or sale price directly in Merchant Center instead of Shopify.

expected_effect.size: price mismatch is a top disapproval cause

risk.note: Never change the product ID; a changed ID resets that listing's history.

steps: Make all price, availability and sale price changes in Shopify, not Merchant Center.
Never change the product ID for an existing listing.
If prices change often, refresh the feed at least every 6 hours and turn on automatic item updates.

test.method: Spot-check price on page vs checkout vs feed for 10 SKUs

title: Fix Merchant Center disapprovals before warnings and limited performance
hypothesis: If we fix disapprovals first every week, then eligible product count recovers faster because a disapproved item cannot serve anywhere until it is fixed.

signal.check: Products > Diagnostics shows disapproved items, or eligible product count dropped recently.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open Products > Diagnostics, filter Disapproved.
For each item, find the cause: missing or wrong GTIN, price mismatch, missing shipping info, policy violation, or formatting or missing attribute.
Autofix only formatting and optional attributes; fix policy, price and required attributes by hand.
Move to Warnings and Limited performance after disapprovals are clear.
Run this check weekly, and at once after any sudden drop in eligible products.

test.method: Track eligible product count and disapproval count week over week

title: Run the checkout and pricing integrity checklist to avoid suspension
hypothesis: If we check payment methods, price and tax display, discount codes and out-of-stock handling on a schedule, then suspension risk drops because misrepresentation is the biggest cause of account suspension.

signal.check: No standing schedule exists to check payment methods, price and tax display, discount codes or stock status.

risk.note: None.

steps: Test every listed payment method at checkout.
Confirm tax and shipping show before payment.
Test all live discount codes.
Confirm out-of-stock items show as sold out and sync to the feed.
Confirm the price on the page equals the price at checkout equals the price in the feed.

test.method: Run the checklist and log pass or fix for each item

title: Run the claims, reviews and site-trust checklist to avoid suspension
hypothesis: If we check for exaggerated claims, fake reviews, broken links and missing legal pages on a schedule, then suspension risk drops because misrepresentation is the biggest thing that hits stores, most of all in health.

signal.check: No standing schedule exists to check claims, reviews, broken links, footer policies, branded email, phone line or SSL.

expected_effect.size: unknown; misrepresentation is the biggest cause, most of all in health categories

risk.note: None.

steps: Check for exaggerated or unsupported claims on the site and in ads.
Check reviews are real, not fake or stale.
Check for broken links from product pages to listings.
Check footer has returns, shipping, terms, privacy, about, contact and subscription management pages.
Check for a branded email, working phone line and sitewide SSL.
Check the theme is not the default theme and there are no dead apps.

test.method: Run the checklist and log pass or fix for each item

title: Work toward the Top Quality Store badge
hypothesis: If we fix the browsing, purchase, shipping, returns and rating components on the Shopping experience scorecard, then conversion rate on listings improves because the Top Quality Store badge has reported at least a 20% lift.

signal.check: The Shopping experience scorecard shows missing or weak components (image quality, load speed, e-wallet options, returns window, store rating).

expected_effect.size: at least a 20% lift reported when the badge lands

risk.note: None.

steps: Open the Shopping experience scorecard in Merchant Center.
Fix browsing (high-res main image plus 8 to 10 more, page load under 2 seconds).
Fix purchase (promotions match the site, several e-wallets accepted).
Fix shipping and returns (30 days or more).
Aim for exceptional on the store rating component.

test.method: Track scorecard status and conversion rate before and after the badge appears

title: Do not claim the small business or any identity attribute unless it is true by Google's definition
hypothesis: If we only claim identity attributes the store actually qualifies for by Google's own definition, then policy risk drops because a false claim is a suspension trigger.

signal.check: The small business or another identity attribute is claimed without checking Google's current eligibility definition.

risk.note: None.

steps: Look up Google's current definition for the small business or other identity attribute.
Check the store actually qualifies before claiming it.
Remove the claim if the store does not clearly qualify.

test.method: Check the attribute is still accurate at each policy review

title: Put the converting search term and product type first in every title, first 70 characters
hypothesis: If we lead titles with the highest-volume converting keyword and product type in the first 70 characters, then Shopping impressions and clicks improve because price, title and image drive about 95% of Shopping performance.
does_not_apply_when: the store is a well-known brand where shoppers search brand plus product

signal.check: A sample of titles shows brand or internal names first, or the converting keyword sits past character 70.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the first 70 characters carry the match

risk.note: A bulk title switch resets learning; roll out in batches, never all at once.

prerequisites: search terms with conversions by product type
steps: Pull the search term report (Shopping and PMax) and list converting terms per product type.
Draft each title: converting keyword plus product type, then variant attributes, then a second keyword or USP, then brand last unless the brand is well known.
Keep titles between 60 and 150 characters, with the searched attributes in the first 70.
Keep one attribute order across the whole catalog.
Push changes through a supplemental feed or edit directly for a small catalog.

test.method: Roll out in batches and compare CTR, CPC and conversion value on changed listings

title: No keyword stuffing, promotional text or false attributes in titles and descriptions
hypothesis: If we keep titles and descriptions readable and accurate, then wasted clicks and policy risk both drop because a wrong attribute sends the wrong searches and stuffing is a policy violation.

signal.check: Titles or descriptions repeat keywords unnaturally, include promotional text, or state an attribute that is not true (for example an aluminum pan description on a non-aluminum pan).

risk.note: None.

steps: Audit titles and descriptions for repeated keywords, promotional language and unsupported attributes.
Rewrite descriptions to front-load real keywords, features, USPs and buyer objections, ending with a plain CTA.
Remove any attribute that is not true for the specific product.

test.method: Re-audit a sample of listings after the rewrite for stuffing or false attributes

title: Roll out title changes in batches with a recorded baseline, never all at once
hypothesis: If we change titles in batches starting with the highest-opportunity products, then Shopping and PMax learning does not reset because a bulk switch across every title resets learning on every campaign.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku with only 1 or 2 listings

signal.check: A title rewrite is planned or in progress for the whole catalog at once, with no batching and no recorded baseline.

expected_effect.size: unknown; avoids the learning reset a bulk switch causes

risk.note: Revert the supplemental feed row for a batch if it underperforms.

prerequisites: a supplemental feed or feed tool to override titles without touching the site
steps: Record a 30-day baseline (impressions, CTR, CPC, conversions, value) per SKU before changing anything.
Roll out title changes in batches, highest-opportunity products first.
Push changes through a supplemental feed rather than editing the primary feed or site.
Check each batch after 2 to 4 weeks before starting the next.

test.method: Compare CTR, CPC and conversion value per batch against its baseline

title: Test lifestyle images against plain white product shots
hypothesis: If we test a lifestyle or elevated background image against a plain white product shot, then Shopping CTR improves for most brands because lifestyle images win the majority of CTR tests, though the reverse can hold for a specific brand.
does_not_apply_when: auto-cropping already damages a supplied image

signal.check: Every listing image is a plain white product shot with no lifestyle or elevated-background test run.

expected_effect.size: lifestyle images won about 90% of CTR tests in one source, though a plain shot won for another brand

risk.note: No text overlays; they violate policy.

prerequisites: high-resolution product and lifestyle images
steps: Prepare a lifestyle or elevated-background image with the product as the clear subject.
Test it against the current plain white shot on a sample of listings.
Supply a 4:5 image through a supplementary feed if auto-cropping distorts the main image.
Keep the winner; do not add text overlays or sale stickers to the image.

test.method: A/B test the two image styles on matched listings
test.read_point: after enough impressions to compare, about 2 to 4 weeks

title: Give every product variant its own GTIN
hypothesis: If we assign a real GTIN to every variant, then each variant listing can target its own keyword pool because a missing or shared GTIN limits how a variant can be found and can trigger disapproval.
does_not_apply_when: fully custom-made products with no GTIN by nature

signal.check: Merchant Center diagnostics flags missing GTINs, or several variants share one GTIN.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: GTINs from the supplier or manufacturer
steps: Check Diagnostics for missing or shared GTINs.
Request the correct GTIN per variant from the supplier.
Update the feed and confirm the disapproval clears.

test.method: Check disapproval count and eligible product count after the fix

title: Use custom labels to carry margin, bestseller and stock priority into campaign structure
hypothesis: If we add custom labels for margin tier, bestseller status, seasonality and stock priority, then Shopping and PMax structure can split by these labels because the split is otherwise impossible to build.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku with only 1 or 2 SKUs

signal.check: The feed carries no custom labels for margin, bestseller status, seasonality or stock priority.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: margin, bestseller and stock priority data per SKU
steps: Decide the label taxonomy: margin tier, bestseller status, seasonality, stock priority.
Add the labels to the feed via Shopify metafields or a feed tool.
Split listing groups or asset groups by these labels in structure.

test.method: Check listing groups can filter correctly by the new labels
test.read_point: after the feed update propagates, about 1 week

title: Never duplicate the same product at several prices to hold more slots
hypothesis: If we avoid duplicating a product at multiple prices to hold more Shopping slots, then duplicate-product and misrepresentation risk drops because the tactic is a policy risk even when it briefly works.
does_not_apply_when: real tiered variants with distinct images and titles, which are fine

signal.check: The same product exists as more than one listing at different prices with no real variant difference.

risk.note: Removing duplicates is safe; pricing strategy needs a brand-level decision first.

steps: Check Products for the same item listed at more than one price.
Remove duplicate listings that are not real variants.
If a pricing strategy needs multiple price points, make them real tiered variants with distinct images and titles.

test.method: Re-check the product list for duplicate non-variant listings

title: Run one feed per currency
hypothesis: If we run a separate feed per currency instead of a converted-price label, then CTR and conversion rate improve because a converted-price label hurts both.
does_not_apply_when: store sells in only one currency

signal.check: Listings in a second market show a converted-price label instead of the local currency.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a separate feed source or feed tool that supports multi-currency
steps: Set up a separate feed for each currency the store sells in.
Link each feed to the matching country's Merchant Center target.
Check listings show local currency, not a converted-price label.

test.method: Compare CTR before and after removing the converted-price label

title: Fix the feed that caused a bad search match, not just the negative keyword
hypothesis: If we fix the title or description that caused a product to match a poor query, then the same wasted-spend pattern stops recurring because the negative keyword alone only plasters one symptom.

signal.check: A product keeps showing for poor-fit search queries even after negatives are added.

risk.note: None.

steps: Add the negative keyword to stop the immediate waste.
Find the title or description text causing the match.
Fix that text so the underlying cause is removed, not just the symptom.

test.method: Watch whether the same query pattern reappears after the feed fix

title: Set local payment methods, language and currency defaults for a mobile-first, non-US market
hypothesis: If we set Merchant Center payment methods, language and currency to local defaults and favour lighter creative, then conversion rate improves in a mobile-first market because the buying experience matches local expectations and data costs.
does_not_apply_when: us

signal.check: Merchant Center payment methods, language or currency still default to a US or generic setting for a mobile-first, non-US market.

expected_effect.size: unknown; not measured in this folder

risk.note: No library source covers this market; verify against brand data before use.

steps: Set Merchant Center language and currency to the local market default.
Confirm local payment methods are listed and shown before payment.
Favour lighter, data-cost-aware creative over heavy video for this market.

test.method: Compare conversion rate before and after setting local defaults

title: Show shipping cost and import duty in the feed for cross-border orders
hypothesis: If we show shipping and duty cost in the feed matching what checkout actually charges, then cart abandonment from surprise costs drops because Merchant Center price and buyer expectation stop mismatching.
does_not_apply_when: store ships only within its home country with no duties

signal.check: Shipping and duty are not shown in the feed or ads for a store that ships across borders with extra cost.

expected_effect.size: unknown; not measured in this folder

risk.note: No library source covers this; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: accurate landed cost or duty calculation at checkout
steps: Confirm checkout calculates and shows shipping and duty accurately.
Match the feed's shown shipping cost to what checkout actually charges.
Re-check after any courier, duty or shipping rate change.

test.method: Compare cart-to-checkout conversion rate before and after showing full landed cost

title: Enrich descriptions with keywords, features and objections, without stuffing
hypothesis: If we front-load descriptions with real keywords, features, USPs and buyer objections and end with a plain CTA, then Shopping and PMax relevance improves because descriptions still matter for match quality even though title, price and image matter most.

signal.check: Descriptions are raw manufacturer copy, too short, or read as a keyword list.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: converting search terms and known buyer objections
steps: Pull converting search terms and known buyer objections.
Write descriptions that front-load real keywords, features and USPs.
Address 1 or 2 buyer objections directly.
End with a plain CTA and no promotional text.

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion rate on rewritten vs original descriptions

title: Refresh the feed at least every 6 hours and turn on automatic item updates when prices change often
hypothesis: If we refresh the feed at least every 6 hours and turn on automatic item updates, then price-mismatch disapprovals drop because the feed no longer lags behind fast price changes.
does_not_apply_when: prices rarely change

signal.check: Prices change often on the site but the feed sync runs once a day or less, or automatic item updates is off.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a feed source or feed tool that supports frequent refresh
steps: Check current feed refresh frequency in Data sources.
Set the refresh schedule to at least every 6 hours if prices change often.
Turn on automatic item updates so Google can pull fresher price and stock signals between scheduled refreshes.

test.method: Track price-mismatch disapprovals before and after increasing refresh frequency

title: Give Shopping the largest share of Google budget for consumer ecommerce
hypothesis: If we give Shopping the largest share of Google spend, then overall Google ROI improves because Shopping is the core surface for consumer ecommerce, typically 60% to 90% of spend.
does_not_apply_when: ecommerce store with a real B2B or bulk-order component, where Search can beat Shopping

signal.check: Search or PMax holds more budget than Shopping despite a normal consumer catalog.

expected_effect.size: Shopping typically runs 60% to 90% of ecommerce Google spend

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Merchant Center linked and feed live
steps: Check current spend share by campaign type.
If Shopping holds less than about 60% of spend with no B2B or bulk-order reason, shift budget toward Shopping.
Recheck the split after each major structure change.

test.method: Track spend share by surface and backend revenue after the shift

title: Launch a new account bottom of funnel first: brand, then bestseller Shopping, then remarketing and PMax
hypothesis: If we launch brand Search, brand Shopping and one non-brand Shopping campaign first, then add remarketing, PMax and Demand Gen later, then early spend is efficient because the account is not spread across every surface before any of them has data.
does_not_apply_when: a Meta-heavy direct response brand with proven creative and little category search demand

signal.check: A new or relaunched account opens with Search, Shopping, PMax and Demand Gen all live on day one.

expected_effect.size: unknown; phase 1 runs about 30 to 60 days on brand plus 1 prospecting Shopping campaign

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: tracking and Merchant Center already live
steps: Phase 1 (30 to 60 days): launch brand Search, brand Shopping, and one bestseller-only non-brand Shopping campaign on manual bidding.
Phase 2 (months 2 to 6): move to Smart Bidding, add PMax and YouTube.
Phase 3 (after 6 months): scale what works.
Exception: a Meta-heavy DR brand with proven creative and little category search can start with Demand Gen instead.

test.method: Track CPA and conversion volume by phase against the plan
test.read_point: at the end of each phase

title: Give every campaign exactly one funnel job and check for overlaps
hypothesis: If we assign one funnel job per campaign and check for overlaps, then wasted internal competition drops because two campaigns chasing the same traffic is a structure fault, not a strategy.

signal.check: Two or more campaigns target the same audience, keywords or products with the same role.

risk.note: None; a role-map audit does not itself change the account.

steps: List every live campaign with its funnel role: brand capture, non-brand acquisition, remarketing, demand creation.
Flag any two campaigns with the same role targeting the same traffic.
Merge or pause overlapping campaigns per the consolidation procedure.

test.method: Run the role-map audit and count overlaps found

title: Default to one campaign per job; require a written reason for every extra split
hypothesis: If we require a written reason for every campaign split, then bidding performance improves because campaigns learn mostly in isolation, and splitting the same products across 3 low-volume campaigns bids worse than 1 high-volume campaign.
does_not_apply_when: a genuine split by brand vs non-brand, country, margin tier, category persona, or a stated commercial need

signal.check: Multiple campaigns hold the same products with no written reason, each at low conversion volume.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 3 campaigns at 50, 20 and 10 conversions a month bid worse than 1 at 90

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: margin by collection, countries, category list, aged stock
steps: List every campaign and write the reason it exists.
Merge any campaign with no clear, written reason into the highest-volume campaign of the same role.
Require a written reason before creating any new split.

test.method: Compare conversion volume and ROAS before and after each merge

title: Run one campaign per country; never two locations in one PMax
hypothesis: If we run one campaign per country, then reporting and bidding both stay clean because a single PMax spanning two locations cannot be read or bid correctly per market.
does_not_apply_when: store sells to only one country

signal.check: A PMax or Shopping campaign targets more than one country at once.

risk.note: None.

steps: Check campaign location settings for more than one country.
Split into one campaign per country.
Use Presence targeting for each.

test.method: Confirm each campaign targets exactly one country

title: Split Shopping campaigns by margin tier when margins spread widely across the catalog
hypothesis: If we split Shopping campaigns into margin tiers when SKU margins vary a lot, then each tier can carry its own ROAS target because a single blended target either overpays for low-margin SKUs or underbids high-margin ones.
does_not_apply_when: margins across SKUs are within about 10% of each other

signal.check: SKU margins vary widely (for example 30% vs 70%) but all products sit in one campaign with one ROAS target.

expected_effect.size: unknown; high-margin tiers can carry a lower ROAS target, low-margin tiers a higher one

risk.note: Splitting too finely can starve each tier of conversion volume; keep tiers at 3 to 5.

prerequisites: margin by SKU or collection
steps: Pull margin by SKU or collection.
If the spread is wide, group into 3 to 5 margin tiers.
If margins are within about 10% of each other, tier by past ROAS and spend instead.
Set each tier's own ROAS target from its own margin.

test.method: Compare blended vs tiered ROAS after the split

title: Start cold campaigns on bestsellers only, not the full catalog
hypothesis: If we launch new Shopping, PMax or Demand Gen campaigns on 5 to 10 bestsellers only, then early efficiency improves because a handful of proven SKUs usually drive most of the revenue.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku with only 1 or 2 products

signal.check: A new cold campaign opens with the full catalog instead of a bestseller subset.

expected_effect.size: about 20% of SKUs can drive about 80% of revenue

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: product-level spend, clicks, conversions and value, or a predicted-bestseller list for a brand-new account
steps: Identify 5 to 10 bestsellers (or predicted winners if there is no sales history yet).
Build the listing group to include only those products; exclude everything else.
Open the full catalog only to warm audiences, or add a separate all-products campaign later to find new bestsellers.

test.method: Compare ROAS and CPA of the bestseller-only launch against a full-catalog baseline

title: Layer Standard Shopping next to PMax for cold growth once PMax plateaus
hypothesis: If we add a Standard Shopping campaign for cold acquisition once PMax stops moving backend revenue on more budget, then growth resumes because Standard Shopping recovers the precision PMax loses at scale.
does_not_apply_when: PMax spend is still under about $15k to $20k a month and still growing backend revenue with budget

signal.check: Raising PMax budget or target no longer moves backend revenue, or PMax spend nears $100k to $300k a month.

expected_effect.size: Standard Shopping can hold 20% to 40% of spend at scale, cold acquisition alongside PMax

risk.note: None; pausing the new Shopping layer restores the prior state.

prerequisites: backend revenue and new vs returning data by campaign
steps: Confirm the PMax plateau with 2 budget steps of about 20% that hold ROAS but leave backend revenue flat.
Launch a Standard Shopping campaign for cold acquisition, brand excluded.
Set its budget and target from the store's own margin and cash, not a copied number.
Judge PMax and the new Shopping campaign together on backend revenue and new customers.

test.method: Track backend revenue and new-customer count before and after layering Standard Shopping

title: Name every campaign with one consistent pattern
hypothesis: If we name every campaign with one pattern (type, geo, focus, optional bid strategy), then account audits and reporting get faster because anyone can read a campaign's role from its name alone.

signal.check: Campaign names are inconsistent or unclear about type, country or focus.

risk.note: Renaming does not affect delivery.

steps: Pick one naming pattern: type | country | focus | optional bid strategy or audience.
Rename every existing campaign to match.
Apply the pattern to every new campaign going forward.

test.method: Check all campaign names follow the pattern at the next audit

title: Kill tiny orphan campaigns and roll their spend into the top campaigns
hypothesis: If we kill tiny campaigns with no clear role and roll their spend into the top campaigns, then account performance improves because only the top few campaigns by spend can actually move the account.

signal.check: A campaign spends a small amount a month (for example under $500) with no clear role.

expected_effect.size: unknown; only the top 5 campaigns by spend can move the account

risk.note: Pause, do not delete, so history is kept.

steps: List campaigns by monthly spend.
Flag any tiny campaign with no clear role.
Pause it and roll its budget into the top-performing campaign of the same role.

test.method: Compare account-level ROAS before and after rolling up orphan spend

title: Turn off Google's auto-apply recommendations and AI-generated assets on every campaign
hypothesis: If we turn off auto-apply recommendations, AI-generated keywords and assets, and auto-created assets, then the store keeps control of spend because Google cannot quietly spend on non-bestseller SKUs or undo a brand exclusion set on purpose.
does_not_apply_when: a deliberate, isolated test of an auto-apply feature

signal.check: Auto-apply recommendations, AI-generated keywords or assets, or video enhancements are still on by default.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open account-level and campaign-level recommendation settings.
Turn off auto-apply for every recommendation type.
Turn off AI-generated keywords and assets, and video enhancements.
In remarketing, turn off optimised targeting unless testing it on purpose.

test.method: Check auto-apply settings are off at the next structure audit

title: Set Sales objective and Purchase-only conversion goal on every new campaign
hypothesis: If we set the Sales objective with Purchase as the only conversion goal on every build, then Smart Bidding chases revenue from the first day instead of a softer goal that does not pay the bills.

signal.check: A campaign is built without the Sales objective, or with more than the Purchase goal attached.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: purchase conversion action already set up as primary
steps: In campaign creation, select the Sales objective.
Skip Google's 'ways to reach your goal' and AI keyword or asset suggestions.
Set the conversion goal to Purchase only.

test.method: Check every new campaign build against this default at launch

title: Turn off Search Partners and Display Network on every Search campaign
hypothesis: If we turn off Search Partners and the Display Network on every Search campaign, then wasted low-quality spend drops because those networks are not the intended surface for a Search campaign.

signal.check: A Search campaign has Search Partners or Display Network turned on.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open Networks settings on every Search campaign.
Turn off Search Partners.
Turn off Display Network.

test.method: Check network settings at the next structure audit

title: Use Presence location targeting by default, not Presence or interest
hypothesis: If we set location targeting to Presence instead of Presence or interest, then wasted spend from out-of-market interest-based clicks drops because only people actually in the target location get served.
does_not_apply_when: Presence is not available for the campaign type in the current UI

signal.check: A campaign's location option is set to Presence or interest instead of Presence.

risk.note: Presence may not be available on Video or PMax in some UI versions; check first.

steps: Open Locations settings on each campaign.
Change the location option to Presence where available.
Note where Presence is unavailable and flag it for a web check.

test.method: Check location option settings at the next structure audit

title: Turn off tablets and TV screens by default, unless the store's own device data says otherwise
hypothesis: If we turn off tablets and TV screens by default and check the store's own device data, then wasted spend on low-converting devices drops because these devices convert poorly for most ecommerce stores.
does_not_apply_when: the store's own device report shows tablets or TV converting well

signal.check: Tablets or TV screens are on by default with no check of the store's own device conversion data.

risk.note: Check the store's own device report before excluding; do not exclude blindly.

prerequisites: device-level conversion data
steps: Pull the device conversion report for the account.
Turn off tablets and TV screens by default.
Turn them back on only if the store's own data shows they convert well.

test.method: Compare CPA before and after excluding weak devices

title: Always separate brand from non-brand in Search, Shopping and PMax
hypothesis: If we separate brand from non-brand traffic in every campaign type, then reported ROAS stops overstating true growth because brand ROAS is structurally high and inflates blended results.
does_not_apply_when: store has no measurable brand search volume

signal.check: Brand and non-brand queries are mixed inside the same campaign, with no separate reporting.

expected_effect.size: one case saw 50% brand overlap before segmenting and 87% brand-unaware purchases after

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: brand name variants and misspellings from search terms
steps: Build brand Search and brand Shopping campaigns.
Attach brand exclusions and negatives to every non-brand and PMax campaign.
Report brand and non-brand performance separately from day one.

test.method: Compare blended vs split ROAS after the separation

title: Exclude brand from every cold campaign with both a brand exclusion list and negative keywords
hypothesis: If we apply both a brand exclusion list and exact-match brand negatives to every cold campaign, then brand leakage stops because neither control alone is foolproof.

signal.check: A cold campaign (PMax, non-brand Shopping, non-brand Search, Demand Gen prospecting) has only one of the two controls, or neither.

risk.note: Re-check monthly for new brand variants; removing exclusions re-creates the leak.

prerequisites: a brand list with all spellings, misspellings and brand plus product phrases
steps: Build the brand list: brand, misspellings, no-space version, brand plus category or product phrases.
Add the brand list as a Brand exclusion on PMax.
Add the same terms as exact-match negative keywords on every cold campaign.
Check search terms weekly for new brand variants and add them.

test.method: Check PMax and non-brand search term insights for brand terms

title: Decide brand Search by checking who actually bids on the brand name
hypothesis: If we check the live SERP and auction insights for brand bidders before deciding on a brand campaign, then brand spend stops being wasted because a brand campaign gives no protection when no one else bids and the organic result already ranks first.

signal.check: A brand Search campaign runs (or is planned) with no check of whether competitors or resellers actually bid on the brand name.

expected_effect.size: unknown; about 1% of revenue in one source when brand protection already works

risk.note: A brand pause test should run 2 to 4 weeks and compare organic clicks plus total brand conversions before deciding.

prerequisites: a live search of the brand name
Auction insights on the brand campaign
steps: Search the brand name live and check who else appears in paid results.
Check Auction insights on the brand campaign for other bidders.
If bidders exist or the account is new, run brand Search at a small, uncapped-on-brand-terms budget.
If no one bids and the organic result always ranks first, test a brand pause for 2 to 4 weeks and compare organic clicks plus total brand conversions and MER.

test.method: Brand pause test comparing organic clicks, total brand conversions and MER before and after

title: Run brand campaigns on manual bidding or impression share, never conversion-based smart bidding
hypothesis: If we keep brand Search on Target Impression Share and brand Shopping on manual CPC, then brand spend stays cheap and controlled because smart bidding on brand terms is not needed and inflates the reported ROAS.

signal.check: A brand campaign runs on a conversion-based smart bidding strategy, or has the customer acquisition setting on.

expected_effect.size: brand Search real CPC often runs 1 to 50 cents on manual or impression-share bidding

risk.note: None.

steps: Set brand Search to Target Impression Share, absolute top, around 95%, with a max CPC cap.
Set brand Shopping to Manual CPC with a low default bid.
Turn the customer acquisition setting off on both.

test.method: Check bid strategy on every brand campaign at the next structure audit

title: Keep brand keywords in exact match, adding phrase match only to find new brand terms
hypothesis: If we keep brand keywords in exact match and use phrase match only to discover new brand variants, then brand spend stays tight because a loose match type on brand terms lets in queries that were never meant to trigger the campaign.

signal.check: Brand keywords run on phrase or broad match as the default, not exact.

risk.note: Do not go overboard with variant keywords; keep the list to the real brand terms.

steps: List brand, misspellings, no-space version, brand plus product word, brand reviews, brand discount code.
Add these in exact match to the brand ad group.
Add a small phrase-match layer only to discover new brand variants, then promote converters to exact.

test.method: Check brand ad group match types at the next structure audit

title: Cap brand spend as a small share of the account for a growth-focused store
hypothesis: If we cap brand spend at roughly 3% to 8% of Google spend for a growth account, then more budget goes to acquiring new customers because brand volume is naturally small and does not need a large budget.
does_not_apply_when: the goal is pure defence rather than growth, where brand can stay uncapped relative to search volume

signal.check: Brand spend runs over about 10% of total Google spend for a growth-focused account.

expected_effect.size: brand about 3% to 8% of spend, 10% at most, for a growth account; 1% to 5% or 0 for Meta-heavy brands

risk.note: Do not cap brand so tightly it starves impression share on brand-intent terms; check R59 coverage first.

steps: Calculate current brand spend as a percent of total Google spend.
If over about 10%, cap the brand campaign budget to bring it down toward 3% to 8%.
Confirm the campaign is not budget-limited on brand-intent terms after capping.

test.method: Track brand spend share and non-brand growth after the cap

title: Check brand campaign impression share actually covers the brand name
hypothesis: If we keep brand Search impression share at absolute top above about 90%, then the campaign delivers real protection because under about 10% to 14% impression share it gives none of the benefit.

signal.check: Brand Search impression share at absolute top sits under about 90%.

risk.note: None.

steps: Check brand Search impression share (absolute top) weekly.
If under about 90%, raise the max CPC cap.
If the campaign is limited by budget on brand-intent terms, raise the brand budget.

test.method: Track impression share weekly until it holds above about 90%

title: Give brand a higher ROAS target than non-brand, and judge growth on non-brand alone
hypothesis: If we set a higher ROAS target for brand and judge growth by non-brand ROAS alone, then budget decisions stop being distorted because brand conversions are less incremental and an account over-indexed on brand looks better than it is.

signal.check: Brand and non-brand share one blended ROAS target, or growth is judged from the blended number.

expected_effect.size: one example: moving 30% of brand spend to non-brand lifted new customers 22% (uncontrolled)

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: brand vs non-brand spend, conversions and value split
steps: Split reporting into brand and non-brand.
Set a higher ROAS target on brand than on non-brand.
Report growth using non-brand ROAS only, not the blended number.

test.method: Track non-brand ROAS and new-customer count as the primary growth read

title: Run a brand Shopping campaign at low priority behind non-brand, with a brand-only negative script
hypothesis: If we run brand Shopping at low priority with non-brand Shopping at high priority and a brand negative list, then true non-brand performance becomes readable because brand queries route correctly instead of mixing into non-brand.
does_not_apply_when: brand product search volume is too small to justify a second Shopping campaign

signal.check: Only one Shopping campaign exists carrying both brand and non-brand queries with no priority split.

risk.note: Watch for non-brand being limited by budget, which lets brand queries spill into it; also check no product is missing from non-brand.

prerequisites: identical product set in both campaigns
steps: Build a non-brand Shopping campaign at High priority with the brand negative list attached.
Build an identical-product brand Shopping campaign at Low priority.
Confirm a brand query is blocked in the High campaign and falls to the Low brand campaign.
Check weekly that non-brand is not limited by budget and no product is missing from it.

test.method: Check search terms in each campaign match its intended role
test.read_point: weekly for the first month, then monthly

title: Exclude existing customers from prospecting campaigns
hypothesis: If we exclude the existing customer list from every prospecting campaign, then reported new-customer ROAS stops being inflated because Google otherwise retargets buyers and takes credit for a sale that was already coming back.
does_not_apply_when: no customer list is available to upload yet

signal.check: Prospecting campaigns (YouTube, PMax, non-brand Shopping and Search) have no customer list exclusion applied.

risk.note: Refresh the customer list monthly; a stale list slowly loses effect.

prerequisites: a customer list export from Shopify or Klaviyo, refreshed monthly
steps: Upload the customer list to Audience manager.
Add the list as an Exclusion on every prospecting campaign.
Refresh the list monthly and confirm the exclusion still applies.

test.method: Compare new-customer share before and after applying the exclusion
test.read_point: 4 weeks after the exclusion is applied

title: Run competitor campaigns only in their own capped campaign, judged on their own conversion rate
hypothesis: If we run competitor-name campaigns in their own separately capped campaign, then the store can judge whether competitor traffic converts without letting it drain budget from proven campaigns.
does_not_apply_when: brand protection already works and non-brand Shopping and Search still need more budget

signal.check: Competitor names are targeted inside a non-brand or general Search campaign instead of their own capped campaign, or not excluded at all.

expected_effect.size: unknown; treated as a waste when brand protection already works

risk.note: Competitor terms can carry legal or trademark risk in some regions; check policy first.

prerequisites: non-brand Shopping and Search already funded
steps: If not running competitor campaigns, exclude competitor names from all other campaigns.
If testing competitor campaigns, build a separate campaign with its own small budget cap.
Judge it on its own conversion rate, not blended with other Search performance.
Pause it if conversion rate does not clear break-even.

test.method: Track the competitor campaign's own conversion rate and CPA against break-even

title: Start a new account on Standard Shopping, not PMax; decline the PMax preselection
hypothesis: If we build the first product campaign as Standard Shopping instead of accepting Google's PMax preselection, then early data stays readable because a new account has no conversion history for PMax to learn from.
does_not_apply_when: the operator has no time to run manual Search and Shopping and needs full automation from day one

signal.check: A new account's first product campaign is PMax, accepted by default during Google's guided setup.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Merchant Center linked
tracking live
steps: Start a new campaign and choose Sales objective.
Decline Google's PMax preselection when offered.
Choose Standard Shopping as the campaign type.

test.method: Confirm the first product campaign built is Standard Shopping, not PMax

title: Launch the first Shopping campaign on bestsellers only, in one ad group
hypothesis: If we launch the first Shopping campaign with only bestsellers in one ad group, then early ROAS is stronger because everything else is excluded until the bestsellers show consistent sales.

signal.check: The first Shopping campaign includes the full catalog instead of a bestseller subset.

risk.note: None.

steps: Create one ad group named Bestsellers with a default max CPC.
Subdivide All products by Item ID and select the bestsellers.
Set Everything else in All products to Exclude.
Add an all-products campaign once bestsellers show consistent sales and ROAS.

test.method: Track ROAS on the bestseller-only launch against a full-catalog baseline

title: Pick a Shopping structure that matches catalog size and margin spread
hypothesis: If we choose the Shopping structure (consolidated, top-seller split, margin tiers, ROAS tiers or labelizer tiers) that matches the store's catalog size and margin spread, then bidding efficiency improves because each structure fits a different store shape.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku or a 5 to 10 product store, which should stay consolidated

signal.check: The Shopping structure was copied from another account instead of matched to this store's own SKU count and margin spread.

risk.note: Restructuring resets some learning; change in stages.

prerequisites: SKU count
margin by SKU or collection
past ROAS by product
steps: Count SKUs and check margin spread across the catalog.
For most DTC brands, keep 1 consolidated campaign.
For a large catalog outside fashion, split top sellers (about 20% of SKUs) from everything else.
For wide margin spread, use 3 to 5 margin tiers; for margins within about 10%, use ROAS tiers instead.
Reserve labelizer tiers for thousands of SKUs only.

test.method: Compare ROAS before and after restructuring to the matched structure

title: Run the Shopping optimisation loop weekly: structure, bidding, negatives, products
hypothesis: If we run structure, bidding, negatives, monitoring, and product-level review as a standing weekly loop, then Shopping performance keeps improving because poor products get fixed and good products get more room to grow.

signal.check: No standing weekly process exists to review Shopping structure, bidding, negatives and product-level performance.

risk.note: None.

steps: Monitor CTR, CPC, conversion rate, ROAS or CPA weekly.
Check search impression share, lost IS (budget), lost IS (rank), click share.
For poor products: read search terms, add negatives, fix title and description.
For good products: if lost IS (budget) is high and at KPI, raise budget; if lost IS (rank) is high, raise CPC or lower tROAS.
If impression share is high but click share is low, fix titles or images.

test.method: Track ROAS and impression share week over week as the loop runs

title: Prune products that spend and click but drag ROAS down
hypothesis: If we exclude products that get real spend and clicks but drag ROAS below break-even, then overall Shopping ROAS improves because that spend can move to products that actually clear the target.

signal.check: Product-level reporting shows SKUs with real spend and clicks but ROAS well under the account's break-even.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no numeric threshold is given, judge against break-even ROAS per product

risk.note: Isolate zero-spend zombies in their own low-budget group rather than deleting them outright.

prerequisites: break-even ROAS per product
steps: Pull product-level spend, clicks and ROAS.
Flag products with real spend and clicks but ROAS under break-even.
Exclude them via listing groups, or isolate zero-spend zombies in their own small-budget group.

test.method: Compare overall Shopping ROAS before and after pruning

title: Pull or de-prioritise a shared product when a competitor discounts it 20% to 30%
hypothesis: If we pull or de-prioritise a shared SKU when a competitor discounts it heavily, then margin holds because matching the price into near-zero margin trades revenue for a loss.
does_not_apply_when: the product is not sold anywhere else at a comparable price

signal.check: A competitor is running a 20% to 30% discount on a product this store also sells, and the store keeps bidding on it at the same target.

risk.note: Reintroduce the product once the competitor's price gap closes.

prerequisites: a way to monitor competitor prices on shared SKUs
steps: Monitor competitor prices on shared SKUs, by hand or with a price-monitoring script.
When a competitor discounts a shared product 20% to 30%, pull or de-prioritise that listing rather than matching the price.
Reintroduce it once the price gap closes.

test.method: Track margin on the affected SKU while the competitor discount runs
test.read_point: while the competitor discount is active, then after it ends

title: Launch one new SKU on its own small budget and listing group, separate from the bestseller cold-start
hypothesis: If we launch a single new SKU into a live account on its own small budget and listing group, then it earns its own data faster because it is not diluted by, or competing with, the existing bestseller campaign.
does_not_apply_when: a brand-new account cold start, which should use the bestseller-only launch instead

signal.check: A new SKU is added directly into the existing bestseller listing group instead of its own small, separate group.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a launch procedure

risk.note: None.

steps: Create a small, separate listing group for the new SKU.
Give it its own small budget, apart from the bestseller campaign.
Let it earn its own spend and conversion data before folding it into the main structure.

test.method: Track the new SKU's own ROAS and conversion volume until it earns a bestseller decision

title: Let converting search terms pick new keywords, then move them into Search, titles and assets
hypothesis: If we run Shopping and PMax broad and read search terms daily, then Search keyword choices improve because converting queries have purchase data behind them, unlike keyword tools alone.

signal.check: New Search keywords are chosen from Keyword Planner or a competitor tool alone, with no cross-check against Shopping or PMax search terms.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Shopping or PMax already running with search term data
steps: Read the Shopping and PMax search term reports daily.
Move converting queries into a Search campaign as exact match.
Feed the same converting terms into titles and ad assets.
Use Keyword Planner and competitor tools only to supply the first rung and extra ideas, not the final list.

test.method: Track conversion rate of keywords sourced from search terms vs from keyword tools

title: Classify Search keywords by intent before bidding on them
hypothesis: If we classify keywords as transactional, commercial, problem-aware, navigational or competitor before bidding, then each gets the right bid, landing page and negatives because a single blended approach treats very different buyer intents the same way.

signal.check: Search keywords are added without a stated intent classification or matching landing page.

risk.note: None.

steps: Classify each keyword: transactional, commercial or comparison, problem-aware, navigational or brand, or competitor.
Send transactional keywords to the product page.
Send commercial or comparison keywords to their own ad groups and comparison pages.
Send problem-aware keywords to an advertorial or category page with the lowest bids and tightest negatives.
Route navigational and competitor terms to the brand campaign or their own capped campaign.

test.method: Compare conversion rate by intent class after routing

title: Group Search keywords into single-theme ad groups, never one keyword per SKU
hypothesis: If we group 3 to 10 keywords per theme into single-collection ad groups, then RSAs get enough volume to exit learning because a single keyword per group can never reach the roughly 250,000 impressions RSAs need to learn.
