signal.check: Ad groups hold a single keyword per SKU (SKAGs), or mix more than one collection's keywords in one group.

expected_effect.size: unknown; RSAs need about 250,000 impressions to exit learning

risk.note: Restructuring ad groups resets some learning; do it in stages.

steps: Group keywords by product or collection theme, 3 to 10 per group.
Never mix 2 collections in one ad group.
Start a new group for any keyword that does not fit the current theme.
Migrate SKAGs into themed groups in stages, not all at once.

test.method: Track ad strength and impressions per ad group before and after regrouping

title: Use exact match on proven converters; use broad match only with smart bidding and proof
hypothesis: If we keep exact match on keywords the store's own search terms already proved convert, and use broad match only with smart bidding and evidence, then wasted spend on unproven queries drops.

signal.check: Broad match is used to guess demand for a new SKU, or combined with Maximize Clicks.

expected_effect.size: about 80% exact plus core broad terms is a common middle ground

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: search terms with conversions
steps: Set proven converting terms to exact match.
Add broad match only where smart bidding is already running and proof of demand exists.
Never use broad match with Maximize Clicks.

test.method: Track wasted spend on non-converting queries by match type

title: Write 7 to 9 RSA headlines built from the store's own offer and bestseller angle
hypothesis: If we write 7 to 9 distinct headlines and 2 to 4 descriptions from the store's own offer and price point instead of chasing a 15-headline ad strength score, then ad relevance improves because real angles beat near-duplicate filler.

signal.check: RSAs are filled to 15 near-duplicate headlines purely to raise the ad strength score.

expected_effect.size: unknown; ad strength is not ad rank

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: the store's own offer, price point and bestseller angle
steps: Write 7 to 9 headlines built from the store's own offer, price point and bestseller angle.
Write 2 to 4 descriptions.
Pin only with a reason: brand authority on brand ads, a must-show promotion, or DKI on problem-aware terms.
Ignore the ad strength score as a target.

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion rate against the previous 15-headline version

title: Fill every relevant ad asset type per asset group, not just account-wide
hypothesis: If we fill sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets and promotion assets per asset group instead of account-wide, then relevance improves because account-wide assets are generic and less matched to each group's theme.

signal.check: Sitelinks, callouts or promotions are set once at the account level and never customized per ad group or asset group.

risk.note: None.

steps: List sitelinks (collections, bestsellers, reviews, promotions), callouts (up to 10, 25 characters each), structured snippets and a promotion asset.
Build these per asset group or ad group, matched to its theme, not just once account-wide.
Skip call and message assets for ecommerce.

test.method: Compare CTR on groups with customized assets vs account-wide defaults

title: Lead RSA headlines with product, price or offer; use descriptions to answer the real objection
hypothesis: If we lead headlines with the product, a price break or a live offer, and use descriptions to answer the shopper's real objection (shipping cost, fit, return window), then conversion rate improves because the ad speaks to what the shopper actually needs to know, not generic urgency.

signal.check: RSA descriptions lean on generic urgency language instead of the store's real shipping, fit or return-window facts.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: known buyer objections for this product
steps: Lead 1 or 2 headlines with the product, a price break, or the live offer.
Write descriptions that answer the shopper's real objection: shipping cost, fit, or return window.
Avoid generic urgency phrases that do not carry real store facts.

test.method: A/B test objection-led descriptions against generic urgency copy
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks after the test starts

title: Fix quality signals before raising a Search bid
hypothesis: If we fix expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience before raising a bid, then CPC falls because the account is winning the auction on quality instead of paying more for the same position.

signal.check: A keyword's bid is being raised without first checking its quality score components.

expected_effect.size: one case saw a keyword's CPC fall from $5.84 to $2.38 after ad and page fixes

risk.note: Landing page experience recovers slowly, over weeks to months, not overnight.

steps: Check expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience for the keyword.
Fix ad copy and asset relevance if CTR or relevance is weak.
Fix the landing page (load speed, mobile checkout friction, promise match) if that component is weak.
Raise the bid only after quality is maxed out.

test.method: Track CPC before and after the quality fix, before touching the bid
test.read_point: weeks to months after the landing page fix

title: Send cold problem-aware Search traffic to an educational page, not a bare buy box
hypothesis: If we send problem-aware search traffic to an advertorial or educational page instead of a bare product page, then conversion rate improves because the shopper is not yet ready for a buy decision when they search the problem, not the product.
does_not_apply_when: the product has no real searched problem behind it, or is a unique low-volume item

signal.check: Problem-aware search terms route directly to a bare product page with no educational content.

expected_effect.size: one case: 3.82% conversion rate, 8.32% CTR, 2.18 ROAS over about 3 weeks on this approach

risk.note: Skip this for a unique, low-volume product with no real category search demand.

prerequisites: an advertorial or educational page
brand exclusion on the campaign
steps: Confirm the product solves a real searched problem.
Build an advertorial or educational landing page for that problem.
Route the problem-aware campaign to it, on Maximize Conversions with brand excluded.
Test exact plus broad match on problem phrasings, with DKI pinned.

test.method: Track conversion rate and ROAS on the problem-aware campaign against the account's break-even

title: Test landing pages from Search continuously with a duplicate-ad rotation
hypothesis: If we duplicate the ad, point the copy at a second landing page, and compare conversion rate over 30 to 60 days, then conversion rate improves over time because the page keeps a standing challenger instead of going stale.
does_not_apply_when: ad group volume is too low to reach a readable sample in 30 to 60 days

signal.check: The same landing page has run unchanged for months with no challenger test.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a second landing page variant to test
enough ad group volume for a 30 to 60 day read
steps: Duplicate the winning ad.
Point the duplicate at a new landing page variant.
Compare conversion rate over 30 to 60 days.
Keep the winner and add a new challenger.

test.method: Compare conversion rate between the current page and the challenger

title: Run DSA only with a large, multi-category content site, after RSAs already run
hypothesis: If we run DSA only on a large content site across many categories, after RSAs are established, then it adds keyword discovery value because DSA on a 1-page funnel just wastes spend on irrelevant pages.
does_not_apply_when: a 1-page funnel or a small site with few categories

signal.check: DSA is running (or planned) on a small or 1-page site, or before RSAs have run at all.

expected_effect.size: unknown; DSA deprecation status should be checked before use

risk.note: DSA status should be checked; one source flags it as being deprecated.

prerequisites: a large, multi-category content site
RSAs already running
steps: Confirm the site has enough content breadth across categories for DSA to add value.
Confirm RSAs are already running and mature.
Add negative ad targets on policy, blog and returns pages.
Check DSA's current availability before building it.

test.method: Track keyword ideas and conversions DSA surfaces beyond existing RSAs

title: Test AI Max for Search only on a cold, brand-excluded campaign
hypothesis: If we test AI Max only on a cold, brand-excluded campaign, then a bad keyword match cannot burn spend on a competitor's line or a discontinued SKU while the store learns how it behaves.
does_not_apply_when: brand campaigns, or any campaign without a brand exclusion already in place

signal.check: AI Max for Search is turned on for a campaign with no brand exclusion, or on a brand campaign.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources disagree on whether to use it at all

risk.note: Turn it off if search term insights show it matching to competitor or discontinued-product queries.

prerequisites: a cold campaign with a brand exclusion already applied
steps: Confirm the test campaign is cold and has a brand exclusion applied.
Turn on AI Max for Search on that campaign only.
Watch search term insights closely for bad matches.
Turn it off if it matches competitor names or discontinued SKUs.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and search term quality with AI Max on vs off

title: Judge CPC against the store's own break-even CPA and AOV, not a general benchmark
hypothesis: If we judge a CPC against this store's own break-even CPA and AOV, then bidding decisions stop chasing the lowest CPC because the same CPC can be profitable at a $150 AOV and unprofitable at a $30 AOV.

signal.check: A CPC is judged as good or bad against a general benchmark instead of this store's own break-even CPA and AOV.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: break-even CPA and AOV
steps: Compute the affordable CPC from break-even CPA and AOV.
Compare every reported CPC against that number, not a general benchmark.
Treat CPC rising with conversion rate flat as the real problem, not CPC rising alone.

test.method: Track CPC against the store's own affordable CPC over time

title: Qualify the account before launching PMax as a conversion campaign
hypothesis: If we check a clean feed, one primary purchase action, a minimum daily budget and enough monthly conversions before launching PMax, then PMax performs better because it is not asked to learn on too little data or too few products.
does_not_apply_when: a hero-SKU account choosing a lean PMax as its only build from the start

signal.check: PMax is planned or already running without a clean feed, without enough monthly conversions, or below the minimum daily budget for the account's scale.

expected_effect.size: about $50 to $100 a day and 30 to 50 conversions a month, or $100 a day and 3x non-brand CPA

risk.note: If unqualified, run manual Search and Shopping instead until the account qualifies.

prerequisites: clean Merchant Center feed
one primary purchase action
non-brand CPA and monthly purchase count
steps: Confirm the feed has no disapprovals.
Confirm exactly one primary purchase action is set.
Confirm the account can fund at least $50 to $100 a day, or $100 a day at 3x non-brand CPA.
Confirm the account has about 30 to 50 conversions a month, or about 100 purchases total.
If any check fails, run manual Search and Shopping instead.

test.method: Track PMax ROAS and new-customer share against the pre-launch qualification checklist

title: Turn off PMax's default settings and add real controls instead of trusting the wizard
hypothesis: If we replace PMax's default settings with brand exclusions, themed asset groups and turned-off auto features, then PMax stops being the enemy of efficient spend because the defaults, not PMax itself, cause most of the waste.

signal.check: A PMax campaign runs mostly on default settings with no brand exclusions, themed asset groups, or auto-feature controls.

risk.note: None.

steps: Add brand exclusions plus brand negatives.
Build asset groups by product type or performance tier with matching listing groups.
Turn off auto-created assets and enhancements.
Turn off tablets and TV.
Set Presence targeting and 1 country per campaign.

test.method: Compare ROAS and new-customer share before and after applying the controls

title: Turn off PMax final URL expansion, or restrict it with URL-contains rules
hypothesis: If we turn off final URL expansion or restrict it with URL-contains rules, then ads stop landing on the wrong pages because unrestricted expansion can send clicks to a size chart, blog post or contact page instead of a sales page.

signal.check: PMax's landing page report shows clicks landing on blog, about, size chart, shipping or contact pages.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open PMax campaign settings and find URL expansion.
Turn it off, or add URL-contains rules plus exclusions for blog, about, size chart, shipping, contact and out-of-stock pages.
Check the landing page report weekly for unwanted destinations.

test.method: Check the landing page report for off-target destinations after the change

title: Turn off PMax auto-created assets and automatic text, image and video enhancements
hypothesis: If we turn off auto-created assets and automatic enhancements, then ad content stays on-brand and predictable because Google otherwise generates its own text, images or video edits without review.

signal.check: Auto-created assets, text customisation, or image and video enhancements are left on in a PMax build.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open campaign settings and find automatically created assets.
Turn off text customisation, auto-created assets and image or video enhancements.
Confirm no auto-generated element appears in ad previews.

test.method: Check settings and ad previews for auto-generated content

title: Build PMax asset groups by product theme, 2 to 20 groups, never one giant group
hypothesis: If we build asset groups by product type or tier instead of one default group holding every product, then PMax performance improves because a simpler, themed structure outperformed 200 to 400 hyper-segmented groups in one comparison.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku with too few products to theme

signal.check: PMax runs on the single default asset group holding every product, or has hundreds of tiny groups.

expected_effect.size: 2 to 5 groups is practical for small to mid accounts, 3 to 20 broadly, at least about 15 products per group

risk.note: Rebuilding asset groups resets some learning.

prerequisites: product type or tier data per SKU
steps: Group products by theme (product type or performance tier).
Build 2 to 5 asset groups for a small to mid account, up to 20 for a larger one.
Keep at least about 15 products per group.
Set the listing group filter to match each group's theme.

test.method: Compare ROAS before and after moving from the default single group to themed groups

title: Never build a single-product PMax asset group
hypothesis: If we require at least about 15 products per PMax asset group, then each group has enough volume to learn because a single-product group cannot generate enough signal on its own.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku, where a whole PMax campaign is built around one product deliberately

signal.check: A PMax asset group is built around a single product.

expected_effect.size: at least about 15 products per group

risk.note: None.

steps: Check every asset group's product count.
Merge any single-product group into a themed group with enough products.
Isolate true underperformers in a shared zombie group instead.

test.method: Confirm no asset group holds a single product at the next structure audit

title: Split PMax campaigns only for a different audience, product line, country or efficiency goal
hypothesis: If we split PMax into more than one campaign only for a genuinely different audience, product line, country or efficiency goal, then each campaign keeps enough conversion volume to learn because an unnecessary split just divides the same data.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku, where 1 PMax plus brand Search and brand Shopping is enough

signal.check: More than one PMax campaign exists with the same audience, products and country and no stated efficiency goal difference.

risk.note: None.

steps: List every PMax campaign with its audience, product line, country and goal.
Merge any campaign that does not differ on one of those 4 dimensions into the main PMax.
For a single hero SKU, run 1 PMax plus brand Search and brand Shopping only.

test.method: Compare conversion volume per campaign before and after the merge

title: Fill PMax asset counts and refresh them every 4 to 6 weeks
hypothesis: If we fill headlines, descriptions, images and refresh every 4 to 6 weeks, then PMax performance holds because stale or thin creative is one of the 5 scaling gates.

signal.check: PMax asset groups run with minimal headlines or images, or have not been refreshed in over 6 weeks.

expected_effect.size: target 15 to 20 images across crops, 5 or more videos, refreshed every 4 to 6 weeks

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a creative supply pipeline
steps: Fill headlines, long headlines and descriptions per asset group.
Supply 15 to 20 images in horizontal, square and vertical crops.
Add videos only if they are strong; otherwise route video budget to Demand Gen.
Replace assets rated low or with no spend every 4 to 6 weeks.

test.method: Track asset-level CTR and spend distribution after each refresh

title: Use first-party lists and proven converting search terms as PMax signals
hypothesis: If we use first-party customer lists and converting search terms as PMax signals at launch, then early targeting is grounded in real data because signals matter most in the first 30 days and fade to a small lever afterward.

signal.check: PMax signals include invented search themes with no conversion history, or signals were never revisited after launch.

expected_effect.size: signals matter most in the first 30 days, then become about a 1% lever on a mature campaign

risk.note: Stop tuning signals after 30 days rather than paying for repeated signal-only audits.

prerequisites: customer list
converting search terms
steps: Add the all-time customer list and top-customer list as signals.
Add search themes built only from converting terms, never invented.
Stop tuning signals after about 30 days of conversion data.
Remove search themes if they start cannibalising a Search campaign.

test.method: Compare early PMax performance with real signals vs invented themes

title: Check PMax for warm-traffic over-crediting before raising its target ROAS
hypothesis: If we check new vs returning share before raising PMax's target, then the store avoids narrowing PMax toward its own past buyers because a tighter target shrinks the campaign toward warm users, not new ones.
does_not_apply_when: new-customer tracking or new vs returning reporting is unavailable

signal.check: PMax's target ROAS is being raised without checking new vs returning share first.

expected_effect.size: 50% or more of PMax conversions can be repeat or warm in some accounts

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: new vs returning customer split by campaign
steps: Pull new vs returning customer share for the PMax campaign.
If mostly returning, lower the target instead of raising it, or move budget to Standard Shopping.
Recheck new vs returning share after any target change.

test.method: Track new-customer share before and after any PMax target change
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks after the target change

title: Test feed-only PMax to push spend toward Shopping and stop drift into video and display
hypothesis: If we run PMax feed-only (no assets, auto-generation and URL expansion off) when it drifts into unwanted placements, then wasted spend on low-value networks drops, though it is a test, not a guaranteed Shopping-only campaign.
does_not_apply_when: the store has strong lifestyle or video creative it wants PMax to use

signal.check: PMax's channel report shows meaningful spend on YouTube, Gmail or Display with falling ROAS, and no strong video or lifestyle creative exists.

expected_effect.size: one case: YouTube 2% to 10% of spend, Gmail about 10%, ROAS down about 20%, fixed by feed-only

risk.note: Feed-only does not guarantee Shopping-only delivery; check the channel report weekly while it runs.

prerequisites: Merchant Center linked, eligible products, correct prices and stock
at least 15 products
steps: Build a new PMax campaign with the listing group set and every asset field left empty.
Turn off auto-created assets, enhancements and final URL expansion.
Leave signals blank.
Add brand exclusions and negatives as usual.
Check channel delivery, product results and new vs returning share weekly.

test.method: Compare channel delivery split and ROAS against the prior full-asset PMax or existing Shopping campaign

title: Keep top-spend PMax products in stock; exclude products that spend without converting
hypothesis: If we keep high-spend products in stock and exclude spend-without-converting SKUs, then PMax performance holds because a product going in and out of stock resets that product's learning and can drag the whole campaign.

signal.check: A high-spend PMax product has gone out of stock recently, or a SKU spends without converting and is not excluded.

expected_effect.size: one case: a product with 15% of PMax spend out of stock 4 days hurt the whole campaign

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: product-level spend and stock status
steps: Check stock status weekly for the top-spend products.
Exclude SKUs that spend without converting via listing groups.
Put underperformers that must stay in a small-budget zombie group instead of removing them.

test.method: Track PMax ROAS around stock-out events for top-spend products

title: Fix PMax inputs in order: feed, brand exclusion, structure, bidding, signals
hypothesis: If we fix PMax inputs in the order feed, brand exclusion, structure, bidding, signals, then time and budget go to the highest-leverage fix first because inputs beat output control every time.

signal.check: A PMax review starts by tweaking bidding or signals before checking feed quality and brand exclusion.

risk.note: None.

steps: Check feed titles, descriptions and images first.
Check brand exclusions next.
Check asset and listing group structure and asset quality.
Check bidding strategy.
Check audience signals and search themes last.

test.method: Track which input level was fixed at each review and the resulting ROAS change

title: Mine PMax search terms to launch dedicated Search campaigns on proven terms
hypothesis: If we mine PMax search term insights for proven converters and build a dedicated Search campaign around them, then the store gains control over high-value queries because PMax takes a large share of search spend but offers less control than Search.

signal.check: PMax search term insights show proven converting queries that have no dedicated Search campaign.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: PMax search term insights access
steps: Pull PMax search term insights for the last 7 and 28 days.
Identify proven converting queries not yet in a Search campaign.
Launch a dedicated Search campaign or ad group around those terms.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and control on the new Search campaign vs the same terms inside PMax

title: Run PMax as a high-target safety net once manual campaigns are rebuilt
hypothesis: If we keep PMax running at a much higher ROAS target than manual campaigns after rebuilding Shopping, Search and Demand Gen, then manual campaigns win most auctions and PMax only catches stragglers.
does_not_apply_when: an account with no time to manage manual campaigns separately from PMax

signal.check: PMax still holds most of the spend after manual Shopping, Search and Demand Gen have been rebuilt and are proven.

expected_effect.size: one example: manual campaigns at 300% to 400% target, PMax at 600% to 700%

risk.note: Requires ongoing management time; only for an account with capacity.

prerequisites: Shopping, Search and Demand Gen already rebuilt
steps: Rebuild Shopping, Search and Demand Gen as manual, well-structured campaigns.
Set PMax's target ROAS well above the manual campaigns' targets.
Watch PMax's spend share weekly and widen the target gap if it still dominates.

test.method: Track PMax spend share and backend revenue after setting the safety-net target

title: Do not rely on Standard Shopping priority to hold back PMax
hypothesis: If we control Shopping vs PMax share through the target ROAS gap and product scope instead of campaign priority, then the split behaves as intended because ad rank, not priority, decides which campaign type wins the auction.

signal.check: The team expects Standard Shopping set to High priority to outrank PMax on the same query.

expected_effect.size: unknown; priority only routes between Shopping campaigns, not against PMax

risk.note: Check Google's current serving rule; it has changed before.

steps: Use priority only for the brand vs non-brand Shopping split.
Control Shopping vs PMax share with the target ROAS gap and product scope (listing group or feed roles) instead.
Read spend share by campaign weekly to confirm the intended split is holding.

test.method: Track spend share between Shopping and PMax after setting the target gap

title: Add YouTube or Demand Gen only after Search and Shopping are dialled in, or with proven Meta creative
hypothesis: If we add YouTube only once Search and Shopping are dialled in, or the brand is Meta-heavy with proven creative and little category search, then it adds real reach because it breaks the search-volume cap instead of cannibalising a channel that is not yet working.
does_not_apply_when: Search and Shopping are not yet dialled in and the brand has no proven Meta creative

signal.check: YouTube or Demand Gen is being added before Search and Shopping show stable performance, with no proven Meta creative to reuse.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Search and Shopping already stable, or proven Meta creative available
steps: Check Search and Shopping are stable and dialled in.
If not, and the brand is Meta-heavy with proven creative and little category search, proceed anyway.
Otherwise wait until Search and Shopping are dialled in before adding YouTube or Demand Gen.

test.method: Track whether YouTube launch followed the gating condition and its resulting CPA

title: Check the YouTube fit before spending: AOV, visual product, creative and budget for 4 to 6 choppy weeks
hypothesis: If we check AOV, whether the product is visually demonstrable, whether a winning Meta creative exists, and budget for 4 to 6 choppy weeks before launching YouTube, then the test is fair because a poor-fit product or an underfunded test cannot show real results.
does_not_apply_when: AOV is under about $25 to $30, which is a poor fit

signal.check: YouTube is planned without checking AOV fit, a visually demonstrable product, a winning Meta creative, or a 4 to 6 week budget.

expected_effect.size: AOV $75 to $100 ideal, over $50 workable, $25 to $30 poor

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: AOV data
a winning Meta creative to test
steps: Check AOV against the $75 to $100 ideal range.
Confirm the product is visually demonstrable on video.
Confirm a winning Meta creative and a validated offer exist.
Budget for 4 to 6 choppy weeks without pulling budget from a working channel.

test.method: Score the fit checklist before committing budget

title: Restrict cold Demand Gen prospecting to in-stream and Shorts, other placements off
hypothesis: If we restrict cold Demand Gen to YouTube in-stream and Shorts only, with in-feed, Discover, Gmail and Display off, then early results stay readable because a clean cold test is not diluted by weaker placements.

signal.check: A cold Demand Gen prospecting campaign has in-feed, Discover, Gmail or Display turned on alongside in-stream and Shorts.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open ad group channel settings on the cold Demand Gen campaign.
Select 'Let me choose' and keep only YouTube in-stream and Shorts.
Turn off in-feed, Discover, Gmail and Display.

test.method: Compare CTR and CPA by placement once results come in

title: Start cold Demand Gen on mobile only when launching with Meta-style vertical creative
hypothesis: If we start a cold Demand Gen campaign on mobile only when the creative is Meta-style vertical video, then early performance holds because the creative format matches the device it is shown on, and other devices can be added once winners emerge.
does_not_apply_when: the launch creative is already 16:9 horizontal

signal.check: A cold Demand Gen campaign launches on all devices with vertical, Meta-style creative from day one.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Meta-style vertical creative
steps: Set device targeting to mobile only for the cold launch.
Add computers and TV, with 16:9 versions of winning creative, once a video proves itself.

test.method: Compare performance by device once winners are identified and 16:9 versions are added

title: Pick a Demand Gen audience approach and never feed it the store's own customer list in prospecting
hypothesis: If we pick either a fully broad, a narrow-then-expand, or a search-theme-based Demand Gen audience approach and always exclude the store's own customers from prospecting, then prospecting results stay honest because feeding it existing buyers just retargets people who would have bought anyway.

signal.check: A Demand Gen prospecting ad group includes the store's own customer or remarketing list as a targeting signal.

risk.note: None.

steps: Choose an audience approach: fully broad, or narrow with a few custom segments and demographic refinement, or open with a few search themes.
Exclude the all-time customer list from every prospecting ad group.
Never use in-market or affinity segments alone; pair them with a real signal.

test.method: Compare new-customer share across the chosen audience approaches

title: Size Demand Gen budget from AOV, not a flat small test amount
hypothesis: If we size Demand Gen budget at roughly 3x AOV a day, then the test gets a fair read because a $50 a day test totalling $500 is not a real test of the channel.

signal.check: Demand Gen is budgeted at a flat small amount (for example $50 a day) regardless of the store's AOV.

expected_effect.size: about 3x AOV a day, or $50 to $100 or more depending on AOV band

risk.note: This increases ad spend; confirm the store can fund a real test before committing.

prerequisites: AOV
steps: Compute 3x AOV a day as the target budget.
If that is not affordable, do not run a token test; wait until it is.
Do not judge a Demand Gen test funded below this level as a real result.

test.method: Confirm budget meets the 3x AOV threshold before reading results

title: Script YouTube creative to hook, then demo, then prove, then ask
hypothesis: If we script Shorts as hook in 1 to 5 seconds, problem, demo, social proof around 60% to 70%, then a strong CTA, then view rate and CTR improve because the structure matches how attention actually holds on video.

signal.check: YouTube or Demand Gen creative has no hook in the first 5 seconds, or skips social proof before the CTA.

risk.note: Never hire an actor to play 'the founder', and avoid lazy AI voiceover.

prerequisites: a video production or UGC pipeline
steps: Open with a hook in the first 1 to 5 seconds naming the situation, not the demographic.
Show the problem, then a demo of the product.
Add social proof around the 60% to 70% mark.
Close with a strong, direct CTA and the offer.
Keep Shorts between 20 and 60 seconds; make a 16:9 version of any winner for in-stream and TV.

test.method: Track hook rate, hold rate and CTR per creative variant
test.read_point: after enough views to compare variants, about 1 to 2 weeks

title: Judge YouTube ads by traffic-light KPIs at the campaign level, not by gut feel per ad
hypothesis: If we judge YouTube using view rate, CTR, dashboard conversion rate and new-customer CPA at the campaign level, then decisions get faster and more consistent because a fixed traffic-light system replaces subjective per-ad judgment.

signal.check: YouTube ads are judged by feel or by individual ad performance instead of a fixed set of traffic-light thresholds at the campaign level.

expected_effect.size: view rate about 20% in-stream, 10% Shorts; CTR over 1% in-stream, 0.6% to 1% Shorts; conversion rate 0.05% or more

risk.note: Judge at the campaign level; ads sequence and one weak ad does not doom the campaign.

prerequisites: view rate, CTR and conversion rate reporting
steps: Track view rate, CTR, dashboard conversion rate and new-customer CPA at the campaign level.
Poor on all: pause. Soft: keep and test a stronger ad. Strong: raise budget fast.
Judge campaign-level new-customer CPA, not each ad in isolation.

test.method: Apply the traffic-light thresholds weekly and log the decision made

title: Wait for a steady CPA over several days before switching Demand Gen to target bidding
hypothesis: If we wait 2 to 4 weeks and confirm a steady CPA over 3 to 5 days before setting a target CPA, then Demand Gen bidding does not lock in a target based on noisy early data.

signal.check: A target CPA is set on Demand Gen before 2 to 4 weeks have passed or before CPA has been steady for several days.

expected_effect.size: switch after 2 to 4 weeks with a steady CPA over 3 to 5 days, or about 50 conversions

risk.note: Raise bids only 5% to 10% (never over 15%) every 5 to 7 days after switching.

steps: Run Maximize Conversions with no target CPA for the first 2 to 4 weeks.
Confirm CPA has been steady for 3 to 5 days, or the campaign has about 50 conversions.
Set the target CPA at or slightly below the current CPA.
Raise bids 5% to 10% every 5 to 7 days after that, never more than 15% at once.

test.method: Track CPA stability before switching and after each bid raise
test.read_point: every 5 to 7 days after the switch

title: Build remarketing lists and wait for size before launching remarketing campaigns
hypothesis: If we build website visitor, cart abandoner, product viewer and past purchaser lists first and wait for them to reach a usable size, then remarketing campaigns launch with enough audience to actually serve.

signal.check: A remarketing campaign is launched before its audience lists exist or before they reach a usable size.

expected_effect.size: roughly 1,000 to 1,500 people to serve reliably, though this is not a universal rule

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: Google Ads tag, Shopify link, GA4 link through Data manager
steps: Build a website visitor list (3 to 7 days, or 30-day default).
Build a cart abandoner list (add_to_cart minus purchase, 30 days or 60 for low traffic).
Build product viewer, YouTube ad viewer and past purchaser lists.
Wait for each list to reach a usable size before launching a campaign against it.

test.method: Check list size in Audience manager before launch

title: Build a cart abandoner remarketing list from GA4 add-to-cart minus purchase
hypothesis: If we build a GA4 audience of add_to_cart minus purchase over 30 days (60 for low traffic), then a real cart abandoner remarketing segment becomes available where none existed before.

signal.check: No cart abandoner audience exists in GA4 or Google Ads.

expected_effect.size: one example: 4.2K shrank to 3.6K after excluding buyers

risk.note: Mark the audience as key so it imports correctly to Google Ads.

prerequisites: GA4 linked to Google Ads
steps: In GA4, create a new audience including add_to_cart and excluding purchase.
Set the window to 30 days, or 60 for a low-traffic store.
Mark it as a key audience so it imports to Google Ads.
Wait for the list to populate before using it in a campaign.

test.method: Check the audience size in Google Ads after import
test.read_point: 1 to 2 days after creation, then weekly

title: Run Display only as remarketing, at a small budget, never as a cold-traffic surface
hypothesis: If we keep Display to remarketing only at $10 to $15 a day, then wasted spend on low-quality placements drops because Display for cold traffic only works at a scale most small DTC stores cannot fund.
does_not_apply_when: a large account able to spend tens of thousands a day testing cold Display

signal.check: A Display campaign targets cold audiences instead of the store's own remarketing lists.

expected_effect.size: $10 to $15 a day for remarketing; cold Display only works at tens of thousands a day

risk.note: Run video remarketing before Display remarketing where possible.

prerequisites: a website visitor remarketing list
steps: Set the Display campaign's audience to the store's own website visitor or all-users data segment.
Set budget to $10 to $15 a day.
Use Maximize Conversion Value, optimised targeting off.
Never target cold audiences on Display below the scale where it can work.

test.method: Track Display ROAS and placement quality after restricting to remarketing

title: Read Demand Gen results by audience and network, then act on the split
hypothesis: If we read Demand Gen performance by audience segment and by network, then budget and creative decisions improve because a winning placement (for example Shorts) and a losing one (for example Display) need very different responses.
does_not_apply_when: audiences and networks are not yet segmented enough to read separately

signal.check: Demand Gen is reported only at the campaign level, with no breakdown by audience segment or network.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one example had Shorts winning and Display losing inside the same campaign

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: segmented audiences already set up
steps: Break down Demand Gen results by audience segment and by network.
Make more creative for the winning placement.
Cut or exclude the weak placement.

test.method: Track CPA by segment and network after acting on the split
test.read_point: 4 weeks after acting on the split

title: Route cold YouTube traffic to a real conversion mechanism and capture email on the page
hypothesis: If we route cold YouTube traffic to a decked-out sales page, advertorial, quiz or listicle and capture email there, then first-order math improves because welcome and post-purchase flows can recover part of the cost even when the first click does not convert.

signal.check: Cold YouTube traffic lands on a bare product page with no email capture, and the store's first-order math ignores flow revenue from that traffic.

expected_effect.size: one case saw a 14.7% pop-up capture rate

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a sales page, advertorial, quiz or listicle page
email and SMS welcome and post-purchase flows
steps: Pick the conversion mechanism in order of preference: decked-out sales page, advertorial (story preferred), quiz funnel, listicle, VSL only at scale.
Add an email capture pop-up or form on the page.
Run a welcome flow and a post-purchase flow for captured emails.
Count that flow revenue in the channel's first-order math.

test.method: Track email capture rate and flow revenue attributable to cold YouTube traffic

title: Cap new-account bids at break-even CPA divided by conversion rate
hypothesis: If we cap manual CPC or Maximize Clicks bids at break-even CPA divided by an assumed conversion rate, then a new account cannot buy clicks it cannot afford once a sale actually happens.
does_not_apply_when: the account already has enough conversion history for value-based bidding

signal.check: A new account or one with no recent conversions runs on manual CPC or Maximize Clicks with no calculated bid cap.

expected_effect.size: one example: a manual cap of about $2 per keyword

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: break-even CPA
an assumed conversion rate
steps: Compute break-even CPA divided by an assumed conversion rate.
Set the manual CPC or Maximize Clicks cap to that number.
Trim the cap by hand as real conversion data builds.

test.method: Track CPC and CPA against the cap as conversions accumulate

title: Move to Maximize Conversion Value once conversions start arriving
hypothesis: If we move from manual or Maximize Clicks to Maximize Conversion Value once conversions start arriving, then Smart Bidding starts optimizing for revenue because ecommerce bids for value most of the time, not for the cheapest product.
does_not_apply_when: order values are fixed, a single SKU, or a subscription, where Maximize Conversions or tCPA fit better

signal.check: A campaign is still on manual CPC or Maximize Clicks despite having about 30 conversions a month.

expected_effect.size: switch points range from about 10 to 30 conversions a month depending on the source

risk.note: Expect 2 to 4 weeks of relearning after the switch.

prerequisites: conversions per campaign over the last 30 days
steps: Count purchase conversions per campaign over the last 30 days.
At about 30 conversions a month, switch to Maximize Conversion Value.
Use Maximize Conversions or tCPA only when order values are fixed, a single SKU, or a subscription.
Launch new campaigns in an existing account here directly, budgeted at about 3 to 4x AOV.

test.method: Compare ROAS before and after the switch, over 2 to 4 weeks

title: Add a Target ROAS only once volume supports it, set at or slightly below actual
hypothesis: If we add a Target ROAS only once a campaign reaches enough monthly conversions and set it at or slightly below the trailing actual, then the campaign holds delivery because a target set far above actual can stop spend almost entirely.
does_not_apply_when: the campaign has not yet reached about 30 to 50 conversions a month

signal.check: A Target ROAS is set on a campaign with too few monthly conversions, or set well above the trailing actual ROAS.

expected_effect.size: switch at about 30 to 50 conversions a month; set the target at or 10% to 15% below trailing actual

risk.note: Hold the new target for 2 to 3 weeks before adjusting again; never set it far above actual.

prerequisites: 30-day conversions and ROAS per campaign
steps: Confirm the campaign has about 30 to 50 conversions a month (50 for PMax).
Read the trailing 30-day actual ROAS.
Set the Target ROAS at or 10% to 15% below that actual.
Hold it for 2 to 3 weeks and check spend does not collapse.

test.method: Track spend and ROAS for 2 to 3 weeks after setting the target
test.read_point: 2 to 3 weeks after setting the target

title: Watch new-customer share before tightening a Target ROAS further
hypothesis: If we check new-customer share before raising a Target ROAS, then the campaign avoids shrinking toward the store's own past buyers, since a tighter target trades reach for stability rather than raising average performance.

signal.check: A Target ROAS is being raised with no check of new-customer share before or after the change.

expected_effect.size: one illustration: raising the target from 400% to 500% moved a campaign from about 4x to 6x reported ROAS but reached less cold traffic

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: new vs returning customer split by campaign
steps: Pull new-customer share before raising a Target ROAS.
Raise the target only if new-customer share can afford to fall.
Recheck new-customer share 2 to 3 weeks after the change.

test.method: Compare new-customer share before and after the target increase

title: Step bid targets gently, never double a budget or halve a target overnight
hypothesis: If we step targets by about 15% to 20% every 2 to 3 weeks instead of making a large overnight change, then delivery stays stable because Smart Bidding needs time to relearn after each change.
does_not_apply_when: a verified outside demand spike with a converting mechanism, where a fast raise is justified

signal.check: A target ROAS or CPA was doubled, halved, or otherwise changed sharply in a single step.

expected_effect.size: step 15% to 20% per move, 2 to 3 weeks apart

risk.note: None.

steps: Change a target or budget by no more than about 15% to 20% at a time.
Wait 2 to 3 weeks between steps.
Watch impression share, conversion volume and new-customer share at each step.

test.method: Track delivery stability after each step vs after a past large change

title: Break a Target ROAS death spiral with an aggressive cut, not a timid one
hypothesis: If we cut the target aggressively once a death spiral starts, then spend recovers because timid cuts leave the campaign stuck shrinking its own audience on a smaller and smaller sample.
does_not_apply_when: the ROAS dip is caused by a stock-out or seasonality that should be fixed first

signal.check: A tROAS campaign's conversions and spend are both trailing off after a ROAS dip, and the response has been a small, timid target cut.

expected_effect.size: one example: 100 conversions falling to 80 a month triggered the pattern

risk.note: Check stock-outs and seasonality first; do not cut into a real supply problem.

steps: Check for a stock-out or seasonal cause first.
If neither explains the dip, cut the target ROAS aggressively, not by a small amount.
Consider a temporary period back on Maximize Conversion Value to rebuild volume.

test.method: Track spend and conversion volume recovery after the aggressive cut

title: Rotate expansive and restrictive bidding, or run a feeder campaign, to reach more cold traffic
hypothesis: If we rotate between Maximize Conversion Value and tROAS periods, or run a low-tROAS cold Shopping campaign beside a high-tROAS PMax, then cold reach grows because staying restrictive forever narrows the account toward its own past buyers.
does_not_apply_when: margin and cash cannot fund a deliberately low-ROAS cold leg

signal.check: The account has stayed on a restrictive tROAS strategy for a long period with no rotation or feeder test.

expected_effect.size: one example: cold Shopping at about 50% tROAS beside PMax at about 600% tROAS

risk.note: No source gives a rotation length or stop rule; set one and write it down.

prerequisites: margin and cash to fund a deliberately low-ROAS cold leg
steps: Confirm the account can fund a deliberately low-ROAS cold leg without harming cash flow.
Build a cold Standard Shopping campaign at a very low tROAS, brand excluded.
Keep PMax at a high tROAS as the warm converter.
Set a test length (for example 60 to 90 days) and a stop rule (for example new-customer CPA above break-even for 4 weeks).
Judge the pair together on backend revenue and new customers, not each campaign's own ROAS.

test.method: Track backend revenue and new-customer count for the pair over the test length
test.read_point: at the end of the stated test length

title: Use a portfolio bid strategy only across campaigns that share one real goal
hypothesis: If we apply a portfolio bid strategy only to campaigns sharing one goal, and add a Max CPC cap or bid floor, then low-volume campaigns share learning safely because pooling different goals or tiny campaigns confuses the shared model.
does_not_apply_when: campaigns being pooled have different goals, such as clearance vs new arrivals, or need manual bids

signal.check: A portfolio bid strategy is applied across campaigns with different goals, or across a campaign that needs manual bidding.

expected_effect.size: one example: CPC spikes to $25 capped down to $9

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a group of low-volume campaigns sharing one real goal
steps: Group campaigns that genuinely share one goal and are too small individually to reach bid maturity.
Apply one portfolio bid strategy with a Max CPC cap or bid floor.
Exclude campaigns needing manual bids, or with different goals, from the group.

test.method: Track CPC spikes and overall ROAS for the pooled group after applying the portfolio strategy

title: Reserve seasonality bid adjustments for short, store-caused spikes only
hypothesis: If we use a seasonality adjustment only for a short spike of 1 to 7 days caused by the store itself, then Smart Bidding does not get pointed at the wrong signal for a recurring calendar event it can already learn on its own.
does_not_apply_when: a recurring calendar event like a holiday, or a spike lasting more than 7 days

signal.check: A seasonality bid adjustment is set for a holiday or a spike expected to last more than 7 days.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: a known, short, store-caused spike such as a flash sale or influencer post
steps: Confirm the spike is store-caused (a flash sale, an influencer post) and expected to last 1 to 7 days.
Apply the seasonality adjustment for that window only.
Never apply it for a holiday or any event expected to run over 7 days.

test.method: Check the adjustment window length against the 7-day rule before applying

title: Try smart bidding exploration before loosening a tROAS target for more auction room
hypothesis: If we try smart bidding exploration on a tROAS Search campaign before loosening the target, then the campaign may find more auction room without giving up its target discipline, though no source reports a result.
does_not_apply_when: the campaign is not on tROAS, or is not a Search campaign

signal.check: A tROAS Search campaign needs more auction room and the only lever considered is loosening the target.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a result

risk.note: Check the feature's current name and availability before use.

steps: Confirm the campaign is a Search campaign on tROAS.
Check the current name and availability of smart bidding exploration.
Turn it on before loosening the target, and compare results.

test.method: Compare auction room and ROAS with exploration on vs the target loosened instead

title: Re-audit legacy tROAS and tCPA targets that a budget cap used to hide
hypothesis: If we re-audit loose legacy tROAS or tCPA targets after a budget-cap behaviour change, then hidden inefficiency surfaces because campaigns that used to be capped now track closer to their stated target.
does_not_apply_when: targets were already reviewed after the change

signal.check: A tROAS or tCPA target has not been reviewed since the 17 Aug 2026 budget-cap behaviour change.

expected_effect.size: unknown; based on a single unverified source claim

risk.note: Verify the claimed change date and behaviour before acting on it.

steps: Check each tROAS or tCPA target's set date against the claimed change date.
Re-verify each old target still reflects real trailing performance.
Adjust any target that now tracks tighter than intended.

test.method: Compare delivery before and after re-auditing legacy targets

title: Size Shopping and Search launch budgets at about 3 to 4x AOV a day
hypothesis: If we size a new Maximize Conversion Value campaign at about 3 to 4x AOV a day, then Smart Bidding gets enough room to find a real conversion pattern instead of being budget-starved from day one.
does_not_apply_when: the store cannot afford to lose this budget while it learns

signal.check: A new Shopping or Search campaign on Maximize Conversion Value launches with a daily budget well under 3x AOV.

risk.note: Start only with a budget the store can afford to lose while learning.

prerequisites: AOV
steps: Compute 3 to 4x AOV as the daily budget target.
Confirm the store can afford to lose this amount during the learning period.
Set the campaign's daily budget to that figure.

test.method: Track spend pacing and conversion volume against this budget level

title: Size a PMax launch budget at $50 to $100 a day and at least 3x non-brand CPA
hypothesis: If we size PMax's launch budget at $50 to $100 a day and at least 3x non-brand CPA, then the campaign has enough room to leave learning because a budget under that floor starves PMax before it can find a pattern.
does_not_apply_when: the account has not yet qualified for PMax at all

signal.check: A PMax campaign launches with a daily budget under $50 a day or under 3x non-brand CPA.

expected_effect.size: $50 to $100 a day, or $100 a day at 3x non-brand CPA

risk.note: Confirm PMax qualification (GAD-095) before committing this budget.

prerequisites: non-brand CPA
steps: Compute 3x non-brand CPA.
Set PMax's daily budget to at least $50 to $100 a day, whichever is higher against the 3x non-brand CPA floor.
Do not launch below this floor.

test.method: Track PMax spend pacing and conversion volume against this budget floor

title: Set budget shares by funnel stage as a starting rule of thumb, then check results
hypothesis: If we start budget shares from a rule of thumb by funnel stage (cold traffic majority, brand small, PMax capped by scale) and then check results, then the account avoids over- or under-funding a stage without needing a perfect formula upfront.

signal.check: Budget shares by campaign type were never set from a rule of thumb and have drifted without a check against results.

expected_effect.size: cold traffic about 80% to 90%, brand 3% to 8%, PMax 20% to 40% at scale, as rough starting shares

risk.note: Treat the shares as a starting point, not a fixed rule; check backend revenue after any change.

steps: Set an initial budget share by stage: cold traffic majority, brand small, PMax scaled to account size.
Track backend revenue and new-customer count as the shares run.
Adjust the shares based on what the store's own results show.

test.method: Track backend revenue and new-customer count against the budget share plan

title: Raise budgets in small weekly steps, cut faster than you raise
hypothesis: If we raise budgets by about 10% to 20% a week and cut faster when a campaign underperforms, then spend grows without shocking Smart Bidding's model.
does_not_apply_when: a verified real demand spike with a converting mechanism justifies a hard raise

signal.check: A budget was raised by more than about 20% in a single step, or a losing campaign's budget was not cut promptly.

expected_effect.size: raise 10% to 20% a week when at or above KPI

risk.note: Cuts can happen at any speed; raises should stay gradual.

steps: Weekly, check ROAS vs break-even, spend vs budget, and lost IS (budget).
If spending 100% of budget and at or above KPI, raise 10% to 20%.
If below break-even, cut budget, faster than any raise would have gone.
Reserve a fast, large raise for a verified real demand spike with a converting mechanism.

test.method: Track ROAS after each budget step to confirm it holds

title: Treat 'limited by budget' as a hint to test, not proof to raise spend
hypothesis: If we test extra spend in steps and watch backend revenue whenever a campaign shows 'limited by budget', then the store avoids overspending on a flag that does not by itself prove more budget will pay off.

signal.check: Budget is raised immediately whenever 'limited by budget' appears, with no step test and no backend revenue check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the flag can appear even at $5,000 to $10,000 a day in a small market

risk.note: None.

steps: Check lost IS (budget) alongside the 'limited by budget' flag.
Raise budget only when the campaign hits KPI and lost IS (budget) is high.
Test the raise in a small step and watch backend revenue, not just in-platform ROAS.

test.method: Compare backend revenue before and after a budget raise triggered by this flag

title: Ignore Google's automated budget forecasts and spend-more recommendations
hypothesis: If we ignore Google's budget forecasts and automatic spend-more recommendations, then budget decisions stay grounded in the store's own break-even and backend data instead of a platform incentive to spend more.

signal.check: A budget decision was made because Google's forecast or recommendation suggested it, without checking the store's own break-even or backend data.

risk.note: None.

steps: Treat every Google budget forecast or recommendation as a suggestion, not a decision.
Check the store's own break-even ROAS or CPA and backend revenue before acting on any recommendation.
Decline the recommendation if it is not backed by the store's own data.

test.method: Track how many budget decisions came from a recommendation vs the store's own data

title: Build the account negative list at the right level, without blocking real product searches
hypothesis: If we put terms irrelevant to the whole business at account level and terms irrelevant to some products at the list, campaign or ad group level, then wasted spend drops without accidentally blocking real product searches.

signal.check: No structured negative list exists, or negatives are added ad hoc without a level (account, list, campaign, ad group) decision.

risk.note: None.

steps: List terms that never belong on this catalog (jobs, free, wholesale, repair parts).
Add terms irrelevant to the whole business at account level.
Add terms irrelevant to only some products at the list, campaign or ad group level.
Review the list for any term that could block a real product search.

test.method: Track search term waste before and after building the structured list

title: Review search terms on a cadence that tightens for new campaigns and loosens once stable
hypothesis: If we review search terms daily for new campaigns, weekly in month 1, and a couple of times a week once stable, then waste gets caught early without over-editing a mature campaign and resetting its learning.

signal.check: Search terms are reviewed on the same cadence regardless of whether the campaign is new or stable, or not reviewed at all.

expected_effect.size: daily for new campaigns and high budgets, weekly in month 1, a couple of times a week once stable

risk.note: Avoid over-editing once stable; each change resets learning a little.

steps: Review search terms daily for new campaigns, new products, or high-budget campaigns.
Review weekly in the first month for normal-budget campaigns.
Move to a couple of times a week once the campaign is stable.
Avoid unnecessary edits once stable.

test.method: Track waste caught per review cycle at each cadence stage

title: Remove clicked, non-converting search terms and promote converting broad terms to exact
hypothesis: If we remove terms with clicks and no conversions and promote converting broad terms to exact match, then cold Search spend gets more efficient because waste is cut and proven winners get locked in.

signal.check: The search term report shows terms with meaningful clicks and zero conversions still active, or converting broad terms not yet promoted to exact.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a minimum click count before removal

risk.note: None.

steps: Open the cold Search search term report.
Add a negative for terms with clicks and no conversions after a reasonable number of clicks.
Add converting broad-match terms as new exact-match keywords.

test.method: Track search term waste and exact-match conversion share after cleanup

title: Build the full PMax exclusion set: brand, URL, SKU, placement, age, customer list
hypothesis: If we build every relevant PMax exclusion layer together instead of just one, then wasted spend and brand risk both drop because a single exclusion type leaves clear gaps for the others to catch.

signal.check: PMax has only some of its exclusion layers applied (for example brand but not URL exclusions, or no age exclusion on an age-bound product).

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: brand list
URL expansion on
customer list
steps: Apply the brand exclusion list and brand negatives (see GAD-065).
Add URL exclusions for blog, about, size chart, shipping, contact, high-bounce and out-of-stock pages if URL expansion is on.
Add SKU exclusions via listing groups for non-converting products.
Add account-level placement exclusions.
Add age exclusions if the product is age-bound.
Add the customer list exclusion on cold campaigns.

test.method: Audit every exclusion layer is present at the next PMax structure check

title: Pass the 5 scaling gates before adding budget or a new campaign type
hypothesis: If we check feed health, tracking, brand split, creative supply and bid maturity before scaling, then new budget actually converts because a failed gate means the account is not ready to use it.

signal.check: Budget or a new campaign type is being added without checking the 5 gates first.

risk.note: A failed gate means invest in inputs, not budget.

steps: Gate 1: confirm feed health, no disapprovals, warnings shrinking.
Gate 2: confirm tracking is validated end to end and reconciled with backend.
Gate 3: confirm brand and non-brand run in separate campaigns, budgets and reports.
Gate 4: confirm creative supply meets the minimum count and refresh cadence.
Gate 5: confirm bid maturity, about 50 conversions a month before tROAS.
Only add budget or a new campaign type once all 5 gates pass.

test.method: Score all 5 gates before every scaling decision

title: Scale only a campaign that already hits target ROAS at its current budget
hypothesis: If we only raise budget on a campaign already hitting its target ROAS, then scaling spend actually grows profit because ROAS naturally falls as spend rises, and total profit and customer count matter more than the ratio alone.

signal.check: Budget is being raised on a campaign that is not currently hitting its target ROAS.

expected_effect.size: 4x ROAS at $100k a month can beat 6x ROAS at $10k a month on total profit

risk.note: None.

steps: Check the campaign is currently hitting its target ROAS at the current budget.
If not, fix the campaign first instead of raising budget.
Judge scaling success on total profit and customer count, not the ROAS ratio alone.

test.method: Track total profit and customer count as budget rises, alongside ROAS

title: Cut fast in steady state, but scale fast on a clear winner or a real demand spike
hypothesis: If we default to cutting fast and scaling slowly, but move fast on a clear winner or a verified demand spike, then the account captures upside without over-committing to noise.

signal.check: The team applies the same slow pace to both routine scaling and a clear, proven winner or demand spike.

risk.note: Verify the winner or the demand spike is real before moving fast.

steps: In steady state, cut underperformers fast and scale winners slowly.
When a campaign is a clear, proven winner, or a real outside demand spike hits, scale it fast instead.
Confirm the spike or winner is real (not noise) before committing a fast raise.

test.method: Track outcomes of fast-scaled winners vs steady-state raises

title: Scale YouTube in order: more budget and creative, then better hooks and offers, then new formats
hypothesis: If we scale YouTube by first adding budget and creative volume, then testing better hooks and offers, then trying new formats, then growth stays orderly because each lever is tried before the next, more disruptive one.

signal.check: YouTube scaling jumps straight to a new format (like in-feed long-form) without first trying more budget, more creative, or better hooks.

risk.note: None.

steps: More: raise budget toward the ceiling and add more creative variants.
Better: test new hooks, 16:9 versions, new offers and CTAs, new mechanisms.
New: try a new format, such as in-feed long-form with a thumbnail.

test.method: Track CPA and volume at each scaling stage before moving to the next

title: Plan stock ahead when a product starts scaling in ads
hypothesis: If we plan stock and supply ahead when a product scales in ads, then ad performance holds because stock churn on a high-spend product resets its learning.

signal.check: A product's ad spend is rising with no corresponding check of stock and supplier lead time.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: supplier lead time
current stock level
steps: When a product's ad spend rises, check its stock level and supplier lead time.
Place a reorder early enough to cover the lead time at the new sales rate.
Flag the product to the ops or sourcing team before it scales further.

test.method: Track stockout incidence for scaling products before and after the planning habit

title: Check catalog breadth before expecting Shopping or PMax to scale further
hypothesis: If we check SKU count against the roughly 30-SKU threshold before expecting more scale, then the team stops chasing scale a thin catalog cannot support, and instead expands the catalog or accepts the hero-SKU ceiling.
does_not_apply_when: hero_sku, where the ceiling is expected and 1 PMax plus brand campaigns is enough

signal.check: The catalog holds under about 30 SKUs and the team expects further scale from Shopping or PMax without adding real products.

risk.note: Do not add thin listings just to add breadth.

steps: Count active SKUs.
If under about 30 and scale has plateaued, weigh adding real products against accepting the current ceiling.
Do not add thin, low-quality listings only to raise SKU count.

test.method: Track scale ceiling against SKU count over time

title: Throttle ad spend on a SKU ahead of a predicted stockout
hypothesis: If we throttle spend on a SKU using the store's own inventory forecast before it actually runs out, then wasted spend and learning resets drop because the campaign never has to react to a stockout that already happened.
does_not_apply_when: the store has no inventory forecasting data showing days of stock left

signal.check: A high-spend SKU is approaching a predicted stockout date with no plan to throttle its ad spend ahead of time.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source covers acting ahead of a stockout

risk.note: No library source gives this procedure; verify against brand data before use.

prerequisites: inventory forecast showing days of stock left
steps: Pull the days-of-stock forecast for high-spend SKUs.
When a SKU is nearing a predicted stockout, lower its budget or exclude it ahead of time.
Restore spend once stock is replenished.

test.method: Compare campaign disruption from stockouts before and after pre-emptive throttling

title: Diagnose a dip top-down: business, channel, campaign, metric, then root cause
hypothesis: If we investigate top-down (business KPIs, channel, campaign type, campaign, metric, sub-metric, trigger, root cause) instead of starting at the metric a client names, then the real cause gets found faster because the fix targets the actual driver, not a symptom.

signal.check: A performance dip is being investigated by jumping straight to a named metric or campaign instead of starting at business KPIs.

risk.note: None.

steps: Start at business KPIs: media mix, what changed outside Google, revenue equation, true KPI vs attributed number, seasonality vs forecast.
If Google is the larger spender or the business dip is unexplained, move to channel and campaign type.
Find the inflection date and check only the top 5 campaigns by spend.
Match the campaign-type failure checklist.
Split the metric into its sub-metric formula.
Write the root-cause sentence before making any fix.

test.method: Track whether each diagnosis followed the top-down order and reached a completed root-cause sentence
test.read_point: at the end of each diagnosis

title: Apply the 3 pre-diagnosis rules before changing anything on a dip
hypothesis: If we check change history, extend the window to 90 to 180 days, and read recent days on conversion-time columns before diagnosing a dip, then the team avoids reacting to a change it just made or a lag artifact instead of a real problem.

signal.check: A dip investigation starts without checking recent change history, without a 90 to 180 day window, or on click-date columns instead of conversion-time.

risk.note: None.

steps: Read recent change history for the ad account, Meta, TikTok and the site.
Extend the window to 90 to 180 days, never a 1-day read.
Switch to conversion-time columns for the last 7 days.
If a batch of recent changes just went in, wait before diagnosing further.

test.method: Check whether the pre-diagnosis rules were applied before any change was made
test.read_point: at the start of every diagnosis

title: Check the bigger spending channel first when Google is a small share of total spend
hypothesis: If we diagnose the bigger-spending channel first when Google holds only 20% to 30% of total spend, then time is not wasted investigating Google for a dip that almost certainly came from somewhere else.
does_not_apply_when: Google holds the majority share of total marketing spend

signal.check: A revenue dip is being diagnosed inside Google Ads first, even though Google is only 20% to 30% of total spend.

risk.note: None.

prerequisites: spend by platform
steps: Check the media mix by spend share.
If Google is 20% to 30% of spend, diagnose the bigger channel first.
Check what changed outside Google: sale ended, Meta creative refresh, offer change, site change.
Split revenue into conversion rate x AOV x sessions to locate the real driver.

test.method: Track how often a Google-first diagnosis found the real cause vs the bigger channel

title: Find the inflection date, then check only the top 5 campaigns by spend
hypothesis: If we find the inflection date on the 90 to 180 day overview graph and then check only the top 5 campaigns by spend, then diagnosis time drops because only a few campaigns can actually move the account.

signal.check: A diagnosis reviews every campaign in the account instead of narrowing to the top 5 by spend after finding the inflection date.

risk.note: None.

steps: Open the 90 to 180 day Overview tab, weekly view, and rotate cost, conversions, value, CPA, ROAS, CTR.
Find the date the metrics clearly changed.
Sort campaigns by cost and check only the top 5 for what changed after that date.

test.method: Track time to root cause using this narrowing method vs a full account review

title: Match the failure-mode checklist to the campaign type that dipped
hypothesis: If we check the specific failure modes for the campaign type that dipped (PMax drift, Shopping feed issues, Search term reallocation), then the cause is found faster because each campaign type fails in its own recognizable ways.

signal.check: A dipping campaign is being investigated with a generic checklist instead of the failure modes specific to its type.

risk.note: None.

steps: For PMax: check warm and cold drift, feed disapprovals or stock-outs on top products, tROAS pushed too high, product bloat.
For Shopping: check tROAS, Merchant Center issues, too many products, search partners.
For Search: check search term reallocation under broad match, a new competitor in auction insights, tROAS, Display left on.

test.method: Track whether the matched checklist found the cause faster than a generic review

title: Split CPA and clicks into their formula parts to find the real cause
hypothesis: If we split CPA into CPC divided by conversion rate and clicks into impressions times CTR, then the exact sub-metric behind a dip becomes visible because a blended metric can hide which half actually moved.

signal.check: A CPA or click-volume change is diagnosed at the blended level without splitting it into CPC/conversion rate or impressions/CTR.

risk.note: None.

steps: Split CPA = CPC / conversion rate.
If CPC is up, check quality score components, new competitors, and premium auctions.
If conversion rate is down, check tracking first, then landing page, audience shift, learning reset, or offer change.
Split clicks = impressions x CTR to find whether the volume drop is impressions or CTR.
If impressions are down, check lost IS (budget) vs lost IS (rank).

test.method: Track which sub-metric explained the dip after splitting the formula

title: Be in the account daily for search terms and anomalies; do product and asset work weekly
hypothesis: If we run daily, weekly and monthly routines with fixed tasks at each level, then the account gets consistent attention because nothing important is left to memory or ad hoc timing.

signal.check: No fixed daily, weekly or monthly routine exists for the account; reviews happen at random or infrequent intervals.

risk.note: None.

steps: Daily (10 to 20 minutes): check spend vs budget, search terms, auction insights, new Merchant Center disapprovals.
Weekly: read conversion-time columns, check PMax products and assets, make budget and target decisions, fix Merchant Center issues, review search ads.
Monthly: refresh search themes and customer lists, review bid strategy for a death spiral, run the policy check, reconcile with backend orders.

test.method: Track how consistently the daily, weekly and monthly tasks are completed

title: Test search ads, feeds and remarketing creative on a standing cadence, never set and forget
hypothesis: If we keep a standing weekly test running against a control on search ads, feeds and remarketing creative, then performance keeps improving because nothing in the account is left untouched indefinitely.

signal.check: No search ad, feed element or remarketing creative has a running test against a control.

risk.note: None.

steps: Keep several ads per ad group and rotate in a challenger weekly.
Replace low-rated PMax assets on the refresh cadence.
Refresh remarketing creative per objection on a standing schedule.

test.method: Track how many active tests are running at any time

title: Prepare the account ahead of a known sale date, not after the sale opens
hypothesis: If we raise budgets, refresh the feed and promotions, and brief creative ahead of a known sale date, then the sale period performs better because disapprovals and promo mismatches do not hit during the peak window.
does_not_apply_when: the store has no fixed sale calendar

signal.check: A known sale date (BFCM, festival sale, anniversary sale) is approaching with no pre-raise budget schedule, feed check or creative brief in place.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no checklist exists in this folder

risk.note: No sourced procedure exists; verify every step against brand data before use.

prerequisites: a known sale calendar
steps: Schedule budget increases ahead of the sale date, not on the day it starts.
Run the feed and promotion checklist before the sale starts.
Brief creative against the sale calendar in advance, not once the sale has opened.

test.method: Compare sale-period performance for a prepared sale vs a reactive one
test.read_point: at the end of the sale period

title: Restructure the account toward fewer, fuller campaigns with a written reason for each
hypothesis: If we list every campaign with its 30-day conversions, ROAS and role, then merge anything with no written reason into the highest-volume campaign of the same role, then bidding performance improves because thin, overlapping campaigns stop splitting the same conversion data.
does_not_apply_when: the account already runs a small, clearly justified set of campaigns

signal.check: Several campaigns share the same products or role, ROAS falls as conversion volume splits across them, and no one can name a business reason for each split.

risk.note: Change in stages, 1 merge at a time, 2 to 4 weeks apart; pause rather than delete so history is kept.

prerequisites: campaign-level 30-day conversions, ROAS, spend and role
steps: List every campaign with 30-day conversions, ROAS, spend and role.
Flag same-product campaigns where ROAS falls as conversion volume splits, campaigns with no role, and tiny campaigns.

For each campaign, write the reason it exists (brand vs non-brand, country, margin or efficiency tier, category or persona, clearance or new arrivals, hero SKU); merge anything with no reason into the highest-volume campaign of the same role.
Where a split must stay but learning is thin, apply a portfolio bid strategy across the group.

Fix the 7 common setup faults while restructuring: GA4 as primary, 1 PMax asset group, broad match with Maximize Clicks, Display on Search, no negatives, auto-apply recommendations on, no naming convention.
Change in stages, 1 merge at a time, 2 to 4 weeks apart, judged on backend revenue.
Pause old campaigns rather than delete them, so history stays intact.

test.method: Compare backend revenue and ROAS before and after each merge stage
test.read_point: 2 to 4 weeks after each merge stage

title: Mine competitor keyword tools for a new account's first keywords
hypothesis: If we mine competitor keywords with tools like Ahrefs, Semrush or SpyFu to seed a brand-new account's first keyword list, then early campaigns launch with more coverage because there is no click data yet to build a search-term-led list.
does_not_apply_when: the account already has enough click and conversion data to mine its own search terms

signal.check: A brand-new Google account has no search term history yet, and Keyword Planner alone is not producing enough usable keywords.

expected_effect.size: unknown, used only for the first keyword list, not proven to add volume

risk.note: No purchase data backs competitor bids; expect some of these keywords to underperform once real data arrives.

prerequisites: a competitor keyword tool such as Ahrefs, Semrush or SpyFu
steps: Run the search-term-led method first: launch Shopping and PMax broad and read what already converts.
Where converting data is too thin, pull competitor keywords and bids from Ahrefs, Semrush or SpyFu.
Add only the competitor keywords that match real buyer intent for this store's products.
Replace competitor-sourced keywords with the store's own converting terms as soon as data arrives.

test.method: Compare cost per conversion of competitor-sourced keywords against search-term-led keywords after 30 days

title: Capture email on cold YouTube landing pages and feed retention into CAC
hypothesis: If a landing page for cold YouTube traffic adds an email pop-up, a welcome flow and a post-purchase or replenishment flow, then the store can afford a higher cost per first order because retention revenue is counted before setting the acquisition cap.
does_not_apply_when: the product has no realistic repeat purchase or upsell path

signal.check: Cold YouTube or Demand Gen traffic lands on a page with no email capture, and the maximum cost per purchase is set from first-order margin alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown, one case saw about 15% pop-up sign-up rate on cold YouTube traffic

risk.note: Adding a pop-up and flows is low risk; do not raise the CAC cap until retention revenue is measured, not assumed.

prerequisites: an email or SMS platform with pop-up and flow tools
a way to measure repeat purchase by acquisition source
steps: Add an email capture pop-up to landing pages that receive cold paid traffic.
Build a welcome flow that leads with a strong first offer.
Build a post-purchase flow and a replenishment email timed to the product's repurchase cycle.
Measure retention revenue by acquisition source before raising the maximum cost per first order.

test.method: Compare 90-day repeat rate and LTV for customers acquired before and after adding the capture and flows

title: Use the real founder or a disclosed spokesperson in founder-style ads
hypothesis: If founder-style video ads use the real founder or a clearly labeled spokesperson instead of a paid actor posing as the founder, then the store avoids a deceptive claim that can damage trust and breaks platform and ecomOS rules against invented claims.

signal.check: A founder-style or origin-story ad is being planned or run with a hired actor presented as the founder.

risk.note: Recasting the ad with the real founder or a disclosed spokesperson is a safe swap.

steps: Check any founder or origin-story ad script and footage for who is shown.
If an actor is presented as the founder, stop the ad or recast it.
Use the real founder, or a spokesperson clearly labeled as a spokesperson, not the founder.
Keep the origin story itself true and checkable.

test.method: Review every founder-style ad before launch for who is on camera and how they are labeled
