title: Use add-to-cart as the primary goal for high-ticket, low-volume products
hypothesis: If a high-ticket, low-volume product optimizes to add-to-cart as its primary conversion instead of purchase, then Smart Bidding gets enough signal to learn, because a $10,000 product with 8 to 20 purchases a month cannot otherwise train the algorithm.
does_not_apply_when: monthly purchase volume already supports optimizing to purchase directly

signal.check: A high-ticket product, roughly $10,000 to $15,000, gets only 8 to 20 purchases a month and Smart Bidding on purchase alone is not learning.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source calls this a rare exception, not the default

risk.note: Optimizing to add-to-cart can fill the funnel with lower-intent traffic; remarket hard to close the gap to purchase.

prerequisites: add-to-cart tracked separately from purchase
a remarketing plan to convert cart adds to purchase
steps: Confirm the product is high-ticket with too few monthly purchases to train Smart Bidding on purchase alone.
Set add-to-cart as the primary conversion action for that campaign only.
Keep purchase as a secondary, observed action.
Build a strong remarketing sequence to convert cart adds into purchases.
Move back to purchase as primary once monthly purchase volume supports it.

test.method: Compare cost per purchase before and after the switch, tracked through remarketing

title: Build a YouTube list of ad viewers to retarget with direct response
hypothesis: If we build a YouTube remarketing list of people who viewed a top-of-funnel video as an ad and then retarget them with direct-response creative, then conversion from that warm pool improves because the follow-up ad matches what they already saw, not a generic prospecting message.
does_not_apply_when: no top-of-funnel or educational video is running yet

signal.check: A top-of-funnel or educational YouTube video is running, but there is no separate remarketing list or ad for people who viewed it as an ad.

risk.note: Building the list is low risk; wait for it to reach a usable size before spending on it.

prerequisites: a top-of-funnel YouTube video already running as an ad
steps: In Audience manager, build a YouTube users list of people who viewed certain videos as ads.
Point it at the top-of-funnel or educational video.
Wait for the list to reach a usable size.
Build a direct-response remarketing ad for this list, separate from the top-of-funnel creative.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of this list against a general site-visitor remarketing list
test.read_point: once the list has enough spend to read, or 30 days

title: Build a high-value customer list as its own lookalike seed
hypothesis: If we build a separate high-value customer list, 3 or more purchases, or top 5% by revenue, and use it only as a lookalike seed, then Demand Gen prospecting finds better new customers because the seed audience is not diluted with one-time or low-value buyers.
does_not_apply_when: the store cannot yet identify repeat or top-revenue customers separately from all customers

signal.check: Only 1 all-customer list exists, and it is used the same way as any lookalike seed would be, mixing one-time and repeat buyers.

risk.note: None; this only adds a second, more selective list.

prerequisites: customer order history with purchase count or revenue per customer
steps: Export customers with 3 or more purchases, or the top 5% by revenue.
Upload this as its own customer list, separate from the full customer list.
Use it only as a lookalike or audience-signal seed, never as a direct remarketing or exclusion list.
Compare results against a lookalike built from the full customer list.

test.method: Compare new-customer CPA between a lookalike from the high-value list and a lookalike from the full list

title: Pick a feed price-presentation strategy when price cannot be cut
hypothesis: If a product's price cannot be cut, then choosing a deliberate price-presentation strategy in the feed, lowest-pack price with an upsell on the landing page, multi-pack with unit-price framing, or a quality or luxury justification, wins more Shopping clicks than showing the single full price with no story.
does_not_apply_when: the product is genuinely the cheapest option in its category already

signal.check: A product's Shopping listing shows only its full price with no pack-size or positioning strategy, next to cheaper competitor listings.

risk.note: Changing which price shows, or how it is framed, is easy to reverse.

prerequisites: pack-size or bundle options, or a clear quality or luxury positioning
steps: Check where this product sits against competitor listings on price.
If it cannot be the cheapest, choose 1 strategy: lead with the smallest pack's lowest price and upsell on the landing page.
Or lead with the largest pack and sell the lower unit price.
Or keep the full price and justify it with quality or luxury framing in title, image and description.
Test the chosen strategy against the plain full-price listing.

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion rate of the new price-presentation strategy against the plain full-price listing

title: Use Search ad price assets to qualify clicks by price point
hypothesis: If we add price assets to Search ads, showing value on low-cost items or the real price on high-priced items, then click quality improves because shoppers self-select before clicking instead of after landing on the page.
does_not_apply_when: the account already fills price assets on every eligible ad

signal.check: Search ads run with no price assets, and high-priced products get clicks from shoppers who bounce once they see the real price.

risk.note: Price assets are easy to add or remove.

steps: For low-cost products, add a price asset showing an entry price to draw clicks.
For high-priced products, add a price asset showing the real price to deter unqualified clicks.
Watch CTR and conversion rate together, not CTR alone, after adding price assets.
Keep price assets only where they raise conversion rate or hold it while lowering wasted clicks.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and CPA before and after adding price assets to high-priced product ad groups

title: Map cart-abandonment remarketing ads to the 5 real objections
hypothesis: If cart-abandonment remarketing ads are built to answer 1 of 5 real objections, complacency, price or value, trust, efficacy, or logistics friction, then remarketing converts better because the ad answers the actual reason someone left instead of repeating the original pitch.
does_not_apply_when: cart abandoner volume is too small to test more than 1 ad

signal.check: Cart-abandonment remarketing runs 1 generic ad instead of ads built around specific objections.

risk.note: Testing objection-based creative does not change targeting or budget on its own.

prerequisites: a cart-abandoner remarketing list of usable size
steps: Build 1 ad for each objection: complacency (offer plus urgency), price or value (comparison or per-unit framing), trust (reviews or third-party badges), efficacy (a real customer result), logistics (clear shipping, returns and warranty terms).
Run all 5 against the cart-abandoner list.
Read which objection's ad converts best.
Add more trust or proof to higher-funnel creative if trust wins, since that means people doubt the store before they even reach the cart.
Share the winning objection with the Meta team so both channels answer the same doubt.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of each objection-based ad against the prior generic remarketing ad
test.read_point: once each ad has enough spend to read, or 30 days

title: Test 3 audience-construction methods in parallel for cold Demand Gen
hypothesis: If cold YouTube Shorts or Demand Gen prospecting runs 3 audience-construction methods in parallel ad groups, search-term custom segments, ICP-website custom segments, and a lookalike from first-party converters, with the same top creative in each, then the account finds which audience method actually works instead of guessing 1 method upfront.
does_not_apply_when: there is no proven Meta creative yet to reuse in each ad group

signal.check: Cold Demand Gen or YouTube Shorts prospecting runs with only 1 audience-construction method and no comparison.

risk.note: Splitting into 3 ad groups is reversible; watch budget so none of the 3 starves.

prerequisites: 2 to 3 proven Meta creatives to reuse
a first-party converter list for the lookalike seed
steps: Build ad group 1 on a custom segment of search terms the ICP uses.
Build ad group 2 on a custom segment of websites the ICP visits before buying, including named competitors.
Build ad group 3 on a lookalike seeded from first-party converters or MVP customers.
Use the same 2 to 3 proven creatives in each ad group.
Exclude the all-time customer list from every ad group.
Read results by ad group after enough spend and keep the audience method that wins.

test.method: Compare CPA and new-customer share across the 3 ad groups after enough spend to read each

title: Run a small YouTube video-view retargeting layer at a Target CPV bid
hypothesis: If a small YouTube video-view remarketing campaign runs on Target CPV bidding around 10 to 30 cents, separate from Demand Gen remarketing and Meta retargeting, then the account gets a cheap extra retargeting touch without competing with the main remarketing budget.
does_not_apply_when: Demand Gen remarketing and Meta retargeting already cover the full remarketing budget the store wants to spend

signal.check: The only video remarketing running is inside Demand Gen or on Meta, with no small dedicated video-view layer.

expected_effect.size: 10 to 30 cents per view; narrower lists cost more

risk.note: Low spend limits downside; watch for overlap with Demand Gen remarketing.

prerequisites: a website-visitor or product-viewer remarketing list
video creative already used elsewhere
steps: Build a video-view campaign targeted at recent website visitors, product viewers, or add-to-cart users.
Bid Target CPV, starting around 10 to 30 cents and adjusting to the list's response.
Keep the budget small and separate from Demand Gen remarketing and Meta retargeting.
Watch for audience overlap with other remarketing campaigns and narrow lists if cost rises.

test.method: Track cost per view and downstream conversions for this layer against Demand Gen remarketing

title: Split ROAS and conversion rate by device with custom columns
hypothesis: If we build custom columns that split ROAS and conversion rate by mobile versus desktop, then device-specific problems get caught early because a blended account number can hide a broken mobile checkout behind a healthy desktop number.

signal.check: Reporting shows only blended ROAS and conversion rate, with no routine device split.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the value is catching a hidden device problem sooner

risk.note: Adding columns has no downside.

steps: Build a custom column for mobile versus desktop conversion rate.
Build a custom column for mobile versus desktop ROAS.
Add both to the standard weekly report.
Investigate the site and checkout on any device that lags the other by a wide margin.

test.method: Check the device split monthly and flag any gap that widens over 2 consecutive periods

title: Match query specificity to the ad surface: category to Search, SKU to Shopping
hypothesis: If broad category queries route to a Search ad landing on the matching collection page, and specific product-level queries are left to Shopping's exact listing, then each query type is served on the surface that answers it best instead of both fighting for the same click.
does_not_apply_when: the store sells only 1 or a few SKUs with no real collection structure

signal.check: Non-branded Search campaigns send both broad category and specific product queries to the same landing page, or Shopping is expected to handle broad category demand alone.

risk.note: This is a landing-page and ad-group mapping change, easy to reverse.

prerequisites: collection pages that match the store's search-term categories
steps: Group non-branded Search keywords by whether they name a category (broad) or a specific product (narrow).
Point category-level ad groups at the matching collection page.
Leave specific product-level queries to Shopping's exact listing instead of building a Search ad group for each.
Review search terms for any specific query still landing on a collection page and fix the mismatch.

test.method: Compare conversion rate on category ad groups before and after routing them to collection pages

title: Gate a non-branded category Search test on proven internal traffic
hypothesis: If a non-branded category Search test only launches when internal data already shows that category gets heavy traffic, using 3 to 5 phrase-match keywords mapped to the matching collection page, then the test avoids wasted spend on categories with no real demand.
does_not_apply_when: no category yet shows heavy proven traffic or interest

signal.check: A non-branded category Search campaign is planned or running for a category with no internal signal that it gets heavy traffic.

risk.note: Easy to pause if the gate is not met.

prerequisites: site analytics or Shopping data showing traffic by category
steps: Check site analytics and Shopping search terms for a category that already gets heavy traffic.
If none qualifies, do not launch the category test yet.
If one qualifies, build 1 ad group with 3 to 5 phrase-match keywords for that category only.
Map the ad group to that category's collection page, not a mixed landing page.
Scale only if data supports it; drop it if not.

test.method: Track spend and conversion rate against the category's proven traffic baseline

title: Match Demand Gen ad groups to the product subset their creative features
hypothesis: If each Demand Gen ad group is built around 1 creative theme and its product filter is restricted to only the products that theme's videos feature, then the ad stays relevant to what it shows, because a catalog-wide product filter can send a UGC video about 1 product to shoppers who land on unrelated items.
does_not_apply_when: the store has only 1 or 2 products, so there is no meaningful subset to isolate

signal.check: A Demand Gen ad group runs UGC or theme-specific video creative but its product filter covers the whole catalog instead of the featured subset.

risk.note: This is a product-filter change inside an existing ad group.

prerequisites: creative organized by product or product line
steps: Group Demand Gen creative by the product or product line it features.
Create 1 ad group per creative theme, with 3 to 5 videos in that theme.
Restrict each ad group's product filter to only the item IDs that theme's videos show.
Keep separate ad groups for image-only and product-feed-only ads rather than mixing formats in 1 ad group.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of theme-matched ad groups against a prior catalog-wide ad group

title: Run a small clearance campaign for aged or grade-C inventory
hypothesis: If aged or grade-C inventory gets its own small, separately budgeted campaign that accepts a poor ROAS, then stock clears faster than a deep discount would, because a low-ROAS ad still recovers more than giving the stock away or writing it off.
does_not_apply_when: the store carries no aged or excess stock

signal.check: Aged or grade-C inventory sits with no dedicated ad spend and would otherwise need an 80% or greater discount to move.

risk.note: Budget is small and capped; the goal is stock clearance, not efficiency.

prerequisites: a way to flag aged or grade-C stock separately from core inventory
steps: List products that are aged, grade-C, or otherwise need heavy discounting to move.
Build a small, separately budgeted Shopping or PMax campaign for just these items.
Accept a lower ROAS target than the main campaigns; judge it on stock cleared, not ROAS.
Pause the campaign once the flagged stock sells through.

test.method: Track units of flagged stock sold and days to clear against the pre-campaign baseline
test.read_point: when the flagged stock sells through, or 60 days

title: Run a dedicated new-arrivals campaign to surface fresh SKUs early
hypothesis: If just-launched products get their own small Shopping campaign instead of waiting inside the main campaign to build data, then new SKUs get seen sooner because they are not competing for budget against proven bestsellers from day 1.
does_not_apply_when: the store rarely launches new SKUs

signal.check: New products are added to the main Shopping or PMax campaign and get little spend because bestsellers already absorb the budget.

risk.note: Small, capped budget limits downside while new SKUs gather data.

prerequisites: a way to flag newly launched SKUs in the feed or by custom label
steps: Tag newly launched SKUs with a custom label.
Build a small, separately budgeted campaign or product group just for new arrivals.
Let it run long enough to gather enough clicks and conversions to judge the product.
Move a proven new arrival into the main bestseller structure once it earns its place, and remove the label.

test.method: Compare time to first meaningful data for new SKUs with and without the dedicated campaign

title: Prioritize Search over Shopping for a bulk or wholesale buyer segment
hypothesis: If a store with a wholesale or bulk-buyer segment prioritizes Search over Shopping for that segment, then those buyers convert better because Shopping's per-unit price display does not match a bulk purchase and drives them away before they click.
does_not_apply_when: the store sells only to individual consumers with no bulk or trade buyers

signal.check: A meaningful share of orders comes from bulk or trade buyers, but all Google spend for that segment runs through Shopping's per-unit listings.

risk.note: This adds a Search campaign; it does not require removing the Shopping campaign.

prerequisites: a way to identify bulk or trade search terms and a landing page suited to bulk buyers
steps: Check the share of orders that are bulk or trade purchases and the search terms they use.
Build a Search campaign with bulk or trade-intent keywords, separate from consumer non-brand Search.
Send it to a landing page built for bulk buyers, not the standard single-unit product page.
Compare its conversion rate and CPA against the same segment's performance inside Shopping.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and CPA of the bulk-intent Search campaign against Shopping's performance for the same buyer segment

title: Tier products by rolling performance and give each tier its own budget
hypothesis: If a large catalog is tiered by rolling performance, such as over-index, on-index, under-index and zero-spend zombies, or high-ROAS, low-ROAS, low-spend and untested, and each tier gets its own budget and bid strategy, then spend flows to proven winners faster because the algorithm is not left to blend strong and weak products together.
does_not_apply_when: the catalog has too few SKUs or too little data to form meaningful tiers

signal.check: A large catalog runs in 1 undifferentiated Shopping or PMax structure with no performance-based tiering.

risk.note: Retiering resets some learning; do it on a set cadence, not constantly.

prerequisites: thousands of SKUs, or a workable smaller set
custom labels or a re-tiering script
steps: Pull 30-day rolling ROAS and spend per product.
Sort products into tiers: for example high-ROAS scalers, low-ROAS underperformers, low-spend or untested, and zero-spend zombies.
Tag each tier with a custom label, or run an automated re-tiering script for very large catalogs.
Give each tier its own campaign or product group, budget and bid strategy.
Re-tier on a fixed cadence, not ad hoc.

test.method: Compare blended ROAS before and after tiering, and track how many products move up a tier each cycle

title: Override auto-cropped Shopping images with a 4:5 supplementary feed
hypothesis: If product photos that get auto-cropped by Google are replaced with a supplementary feed of 4:5 images, then Shopping listings look correct and click better because the auto-crop no longer cuts off part of the product or the model.
does_not_apply_when: source images are already 4:5 or the current crop looks correct

signal.check: Product images in a wide or non-4:5 ratio are being auto-cropped by Google in the Shopping listing.

risk.note: A supplementary feed can be removed without touching the primary feed.

prerequisites: source images or the ability to re-crop them to 4:5
steps: Check current Shopping listings for images that look auto-cropped or cut off.
Prepare a 4:5 version of each affected product image.
Load the 4:5 images through a supplementary feed, without changing the primary feed.
Compare CTR on the corrected listings against the prior auto-cropped versions.

test.method: Compare CTR before and after the 4:5 supplementary feed goes live on affected products

title: Build a permanent account-level negative list for junk search terms
hypothesis: If a permanent account-level negative keyword list for generic junk terms, such as jobs, careers, interns and salary, is applied once, then every future campaign inherits it automatically because it works at the account level instead of being rebuilt per campaign.

signal.check: New campaigns pick up generic junk clicks, jobs, careers, salary and similar terms, that a shared account-level list would already block.

risk.note: A shared list is easy to edit or remove later.

steps: Build a shared negative keyword list of generic junk terms: jobs, careers, interns, salary, and similar.
Apply it at the account level so every campaign, current and future, inherits it.
Review it a few times a year and add newly discovered junk terms.
Do not rebuild this list per campaign.

test.method: Check wasted spend on junk terms before and after the account-level list goes live
test.read_point: 30 days after the list is applied

title: Default to an isolated fix over a rebuild when diagnosing a dip
hypothesis: If a diagnosed performance dip is answered with 1 isolated fix by default, and a full rebuild only when isolated fixes fail to close the gap or the dip is severe enough to justify a multi-fix response, then the team learns what actually worked instead of resetting learning with an unnecessary rebuild.

signal.check: A performance dip is being answered with a full campaign or account rebuild before an isolated fix has been tried.

risk.note: A rebuild resets learning and is not easily undone; reserve it for when isolated fixes fail.

prerequisites: a completed root-cause diagnosis before choosing a response
steps: State the full root-cause sentence for the dip before choosing any fix.
Assess severity: mild dip gets 1 isolated fix; a dire dip can justify several fixes at once.
Apply the smallest fix that is honestly big enough to close the gap.
Wait long enough, scaled to conversion volume, to see if the fix worked before layering another.
Only consider a full rebuild if isolated fixes fail or cannot close the gap to historical performance.

test.method: Track whether the applied fix closed the gap to historical performance before any further change
test.read_point: sized to the campaign's conversion volume, typically 2 to 4 weeks

title: Duplicate the feed into role-specific versions for Shopping and PMax
hypothesis: If the product feed is duplicated into 2 supplemental versions, one tuned for Shopping's branded and high-intent category terms and one tuned for PMax's discovery and scaling, then the 2 campaign types stop cannibalizing each other on the same titles because each reads a feed built for its own job.
does_not_apply_when: the account runs only 1 of Shopping or PMax, not both

signal.check: Standard Shopping and PMax both read the same primary feed with no role-specific differences, and the 2 compete for the same queries.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the source gives no method for how the 2 versions should differ

risk.note: Supplemental feeds do not touch the site or the primary feed.

prerequisites: a supplemental feed tool such as Channable or a Merchant Center supplemental feed
steps: Create a supplemental feed for Shopping, tuned toward branded and high-intent category terms.
Create a second supplemental feed for PMax, tuned toward discovery and scaling terms.
Do not edit the site or the primary feed.
Watch for the same product still serving twice on the same query, and adjust the rules if it does.

test.method: Compare cannibalization, shared query overlap, and blended ROAS before and after the feed split

title: Test a brand-first title order for verticals where it may beat brand-last
hypothesis: If fashion, electronics or seasonal listings test a brand-first title order, brand plus product type plus key feature, model or size, instead of the default converting-keyword-first order, then some verticals may perform better because shoppers in those categories search by brand or model more than in general retail.
does_not_apply_when: the brand is unknown to most shoppers in that category

signal.check: Every product title uses the default converting-keyword-first, brand-last order with no vertical exceptions tested.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the source does not say which verticals benefit

risk.note: Title order can be reverted; test on a subset before a catalog-wide change.

steps: Pick a fashion, electronics or seasonal category as a test subset.
Rebuild titles for that subset with brand first, then product type, key feature, model or size.
Keep the converting-keyword-first order on the rest of the catalog as the control.
Compare CTR and conversion rate on the test subset against its own baseline.
Roll out only if the brand-first order wins; otherwise keep the default order.

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion rate of the brand-first subset against its pre-change baseline

title: Split PMax into a prospecting campaign and a remarketing or brand-defense campaign
hypothesis: If PMax is split into 1 prospecting campaign with broad signals and a high-priority feed and 1 remarketing or brand-defense campaign with different asset groups and audience signals, then prospecting stops being starved of data by brand-driven and warm conversions inside the same campaign.
does_not_apply_when: the account is too small to support 2 PMax campaigns with enough data each

signal.check: 1 PMax campaign is asked to do both cold prospecting and warm remarketing or brand defense at once.

expected_effect.size: unknown, this sits in tension with excluding brand from PMax entirely, so test carefully

risk.note: Watch for the brand-defense PMax re-absorbing traffic meant for a dedicated brand Search or Shopping campaign.

prerequisites: enough conversion volume to support 2 PMax campaigns
steps: Build a prospecting PMax with broad signals and a high-priority feed, brand excluded.
Build a second PMax for remarketing or brand defense, with its own asset groups and audience signals.
Keep brand exclusions and negatives on the prospecting PMax only.
Watch new versus returning customer share in each campaign separately.

test.method: Track new-customer ROAS in the prospecting PMax before and after the split

title: Forecast before scaling Demand Gen with Performance Planner and the tCPA simulator
hypothesis: If Google's Performance Planner or Reach Planner and the tCPA Scaling Simulator are used to forecast traffic and cost before raising a Demand Gen bid or budget, then scaling decisions are based on a forecast instead of a guess about what a bigger bid or budget will do.

signal.check: Demand Gen bids or budgets are being raised with no forecast of expected traffic or cost change.

risk.note: Forecasting adds a check step; it does not change the campaign on its own.

prerequisites: access to Performance Planner, Reach Planner or the tCPA Scaling Simulator in the account
steps: Before raising a Demand Gen bid or budget, open Performance Planner or Reach Planner for a forecast.
For a bid increase, run the in-platform tCPA Scaling Simulator to forecast traffic and cost.
Compare the forecast against the account's break-even CPA before applying the change.
Make the change only if the forecast still clears break-even.

test.method: Compare the forecast to the actual result after the change goes live

title: Pool same-currency countries into one MCC-level portfolio bid strategy
hypothesis: If campaigns from several countries that share a currency are pooled into 1 MCC-level portfolio bid strategy, then small markets get enough conversion volume to bid well because their data is pooled with larger markets instead of each learning alone.
does_not_apply_when: countries in the pool use different currencies, or 1 country's volume would swamp the others' learning

signal.check: Several small-market campaigns in the same currency each run their own bid strategy with too little volume to learn well.

risk.note: Watch that a large market does not dominate the pooled bid at the expense of small markets.

prerequisites: multiple country campaigns sharing 1 currency inside the same MCC
steps: Confirm which country campaigns share 1 currency inside the MCC.
Group only campaigns with 1 shared goal into an MCC-level portfolio bid strategy.
Watch each country's individual results after pooling, not only the pooled average.
Split a country back out if it is being dominated by a larger market's pattern.

test.method: Compare small-market CPA before and after pooling into the portfolio strategy

title: Build real tiered product variants to legitimately hold more Shopping slots
hypothesis: If a proven bestseller is rebuilt as genuinely different tiered listings, a real price tier, a distinct avatar or use-case image, and a title and description aimed at that tier's keywords, then the store can legitimately hold more Shopping slots for the same demand, because each listing is a real, differentiated product rather than a relisted duplicate.
does_not_apply_when: the store cannot support real pricing, packaging or positioning differences between the variants

signal.check: 1 proven bestseller holds only 1 Shopping slot for its demand, and the store has real variant options, price tier, use case, packaging, it has not built as separate listings.

expected_effect.size: unknown, do not relist the same item at different prices to fake this

risk.note: Real, distinct variants are fine; relisting the same item at multiple prices is a policy and trust risk, see GAD-042.

prerequisites: a real basis for tiered variants: different pack size, tier, or use case, not the same item relisted
steps: Pick 1 product that already converts well.
Define 2 to 5 real variants: a genuine price tier, packaging difference, or use-case version, not the same item at a different price.
Give each variant its own image built for its use case or avatar.
Write each variant's title and description toward its own keyword pool.
Check Merchant Center policy on duplicate and misrepresentation rules before publishing.

test.method: Track combined slot share and combined conversion value across the variants versus the single original listing

title: Offer a free-plus-shipping entry product that leads into the catalog
hypothesis: If an entry product is offered free plus shipping, chosen because it naturally leads into the store's other products rather than ending the relationship, then new customers enter the ecosystem cheaply and convert into paying customers through the follow-up remarketing, email and SMS sequence.
does_not_apply_when: cash flow cannot fund giving a product away before follow-on revenue arrives

signal.check: There is no low-cost or free entry offer bringing new people into the store's remarketing, email or SMS list.

risk.note: Check cash flow and expected follow-on purchase rate before launch; this is a real product cost, not a discount.

prerequisites: a product that naturally leads to further purchases
cash flow to cover the free product and shipping
steps: Pick an entry product that starts a need for other products in the catalog, not one that ends it.
Offer it free, with the customer paying only shipping.
Check cash flow can cover the product and shipping cost before launch.
Follow up with remarketing, email and SMS to sell the related products.
Track how many free-offer customers convert to a paid order and over what time.

test.method: Track conversion rate from free-offer customer to first paid order, and time to that order

title: Use full-catalog dynamic remarketing for warm audiences
hypothesis: If warm audiences, site visitors, cart adders and past buyers, see full-catalog dynamic product remarketing instead of a narrow bestseller set, then they convert better because each person sees the specific product they viewed or added, not a generic storewide pick.
does_not_apply_when: the store has too few warm visitors to populate a dynamic remarketing list

signal.check: Remarketing to site visitors, cart adders or past buyers shows the same narrow bestseller set used for cold traffic instead of the specific product each person viewed or carted.

risk.note: This only changes what warm remarketing shows, not cold-traffic targeting.

prerequisites: product-level remarketing tags, product ID and category, already firing
steps: Confirm the whole catalog, not just bestsellers, is eligible for dynamic remarketing.
Build remarketing audiences for product viewers, cart adders and past buyers.
Let Google's dynamic remarketing show each person the product they viewed, added or are likely to want next.
Sell the wider range to these warm audiences through email and SMS as well as ads.
Keep cold-traffic campaigns narrowed to bestsellers, since this rule is for warm traffic only.

test.method: Compare conversion rate of full-catalog dynamic remarketing against the prior narrow-set remarketing

title: Build a fuller Demand Gen retargeting audience taxonomy
hypothesis: If Demand Gen retargeting is split into distinct segments, product page viewers, cart adders without purchase, abandoned checkout, category viewers, all site visitors, and past purchasers for upsell, instead of 1 broad remarketing list, then each segment gets creative and budget matched to how close it is to buying.
does_not_apply_when: site traffic is too low to populate more than 1 or 2 usable segments

signal.check: Demand Gen or Display remarketing runs on 1 broad all-visitor list instead of segments split by funnel depth.

risk.note: Segments can be merged back if any is too small to read.

prerequisites: product view, add-to-cart and checkout-start events tagged separately
steps: Build 6 segments: product page viewers, cart adders without purchase, abandoned checkout, category page viewers, all site visitors, and past purchasers.
Give each segment its own ad group or campaign and its own creative.
Read ROAS, spend and clicks by segment, not blended.
Move budget toward the segments that convert best and cut or merge the ones too small or too weak to read.

test.method: Compare ROAS by segment against the prior single broad remarketing list

title: Audit PMax's own spend split before rebuilding it into manual campaigns
hypothesis: If an operator audits where PMax currently spends, Shopping, Search text, or image and video, before rebuilding it into separate manual campaigns, and rebuilds in that order, then the rebuild targets the highest-spend surface first instead of guessing which campaign type to build first.
does_not_apply_when: the account is staying on PMax and not rebuilding it into manual campaigns

signal.check: A team is planning to rebuild PMax into Standard Shopping, Search and Demand Gen with no check on where PMax's spend currently goes.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the goal is a better-sequenced rebuild, not more spend

risk.note: This is a planning step before the rebuild, not a change on its own.

prerequisites: PMax channel or placement reporting turned on
steps: Pull PMax spend and conversion value by channel: Shopping, Search text, and image and video.
Rank the channels by PMax spend share.
Build the replacement manual campaign for the highest-spend channel first, usually Standard Shopping.
Build Search next, then Demand Gen, following the same spend-ranked order.
Keep PMax running at a much higher ROAS target as a safety net throughout the rebuild.

test.method: Track manual campaign volume against PMax's prior channel-level spend as each piece launches
test.read_point: after each rebuild stage, over about 90 days total

title: Judge an assist layer by downstream lag, not its own last-click ROAS
hypothesis: If a top-of-funnel assist layer such as Demand Gen is judged by its effect on downstream branded and direct performance over several weeks instead of its own last-click ROAS, then the account avoids cutting a layer that looks weak alone but is quietly feeding the campaigns that do convert.
does_not_apply_when: the account cannot isolate a test window to compare branded performance with and without the assist layer

signal.check: A top-of-funnel or assist campaign is being judged, or cut, on its own last-click ROAS alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source reports a lagged drop in branded performance weeks after cutting the assist layer, with no test design given

risk.note: Pausing an assist layer to test its effect can cost real branded and direct performance for the test window.

prerequisites: branded and non-brand performance tracked separately
a willingness to run a pause or reduction test
steps: Record baseline branded and non-brand Search and Shopping performance.
Pause or sharply reduce the assist layer for a set test window.
Watch branded and non-brand performance over the following weeks, not just the assist layer's own numbers.
Resume the assist layer if downstream performance drops, and treat that drop as its real value.
Judge the assist layer by this downstream effect going forward, not by its own last-click ROAS.

test.method: Compare branded and non-brand performance for several weeks with the assist layer off against the prior baseline
test.read_point: 4 to 8 weeks after pausing the assist layer

title: Check 4 fixed GA4 reports every 2 weeks for paid traffic health
hypothesis: If the team checks 4 fixed GA4 reports every couple of weeks, user attributes, ecommerce purchases by product, the landing page report, and channel plus source and medium, then problems in paid traffic quality or landing pages get caught on a schedule instead of only when someone happens to look.
does_not_apply_when: GA4 is not the store's analytics platform

signal.check: No routine cadence exists for checking GA4's user, ecommerce, landing page and channel reports for paid traffic.

risk.note: This is a reporting habit, not a change to campaigns.

prerequisites: GA4 linked to Google Ads with UTM parameters on paid traffic
steps: Every 2 weeks, check the user attributes report for who paid traffic actually reaches.
Check the ecommerce purchases report for views, add-to-carts and purchases per product.
Check the landing page report for sessions, engagement time and bounce rate on pages that receive paid traffic.
Check the channel and source and medium report to confirm paid traffic is tagged and counted correctly.

test.method: Track whether this cadence catches a landing page or tagging problem before it shows up in Google Ads reporting

title: Fix landing page speed and fulfilment reliability to cut Google's experience penalty
hypothesis: If landing page speed and order fulfilment reliability improve, then Google's ad-rank experience penalty falls over time, which lowers CPC and raises rank, because the auction rewards fast pages and reliable delivery as much as bid and relevance.

signal.check: Ad landing pages load slowly, or shipping and delivery are unreliable, while CPC trends up with no clear bid or competitor cause.

expected_effect.size: unknown, source says the effect builds over weeks to months, not immediately

risk.note: Speed and fulfilment fixes carry no ad-account risk; they are site and ops work.

prerequisites: page speed measurement on ad landing pages
on-time shipment tracking
steps: Measure page speed on the specific landing pages ads send traffic to, not just the homepage.
Fix the slowest ad landing pages first.
Check on-time shipment and order-fulfilment rates for products running in ads.
Track CPC and rank on the same keywords or products over the following weeks as speed and fulfilment improve.

test.method: Track CPC and quality-related metrics on the same keywords or products before and after the speed and fulfilment fixes

title: Build a founder personal brand or tell the origin story in ads
hypothesis: If a willing founder builds a public personal brand, or at minimum the ads tell a true origin story of why the product was made, then ads convert better on comparison because personal brand acts as trust at scale when a buyer weighs the store against a competitor.
does_not_apply_when: no founder or owner is willing or able to appear in ads or be public

signal.check: Ads carry no founder presence and no origin story, and the brand competes mainly on product claims alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 1 anecdote reports 2x versus 6x ROAS between similar businesses, confounded by spend level

risk.note: Telling a true origin story is low risk; building a public personal following is a bigger, longer-term commitment.

prerequisites: a true, checkable origin story or a founder willing to be public
steps: Decide whether the founder or owner can and wants to build a public following.
If yes, invest time in the founder's own following and use it in ad creative.
If no, write the origin story: why the product was made, in the founder's own words.
Use the origin story in ad copy and creative, especially where buyers compare the store to a competitor.
Keep every claim in the story true and checkable.

test.method: Compare ROAS or conversion rate of ads with founder or origin-story creative against ads without it
